title.rendered: Most Influential Women in the World: 15 Women Who Changed History

content.rendered:
Quick answer first, then the detailed list — 15 women whose documented work changed the world they lived in: scientists, aviators, activists, artists, heads of government, a media builder, a tennis champion and a finance minister. Each entry has a verified photograph, the achievement she is known for, and an honest account of why it mattered.

This is an editorial selection, not an official ranking — influence has no governing body and no championship, and any list of "the most influential" is an argument, not a measurement. So instead of pretending to rank these fifteen against each other, this guide explains what each of them actually did, and lets the record make the case. The order is broadly chronological, moving from the trailblazers of the twentieth century to the women shaping the present one.

A note on honesty: every date, office and achievement below is drawn from reputable published references — encyclopaedia entries, official biographies and broadsheet reporting — checked as of October 2026, so that offices are stated as they stand now, not as they stood when a famous photograph was taken. Every photograph is a real, identity-checked photograph of the woman herself from Wikimedia Commons, credited in full in our research note at the end.

Quick Answer: The 15 Women at a Glance

For science, start with Marie Curie, the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, and Jane Goodall, whose chimpanzee research rewrote our understanding of animals. For courage in the face of power, read Rosa Parks and Malala Yousafzai. For the exercise of power itself: Indira Gandhi, Angela Merkel, Ursula von der Leyen, Kamala Harris, Jacinda Ardern and Nirmala Sitharaman. For influence built outside office, see Amelia Earhart, Frida Kahlo, Mother Teresa, Oprah Winfrey and Serena Williams.

What "Influence" Means in This List

Influence is easy to claim and hard to define, so this list uses one test: documented impact that outlasts the moment. A discovery that founded a science. A protest that became a movement. An office held long enough, or a barrier broken clearly enough, to change what successors could attempt. A body of work — paintings, broadcasts, matches — that altered its field's economics and expectations. Fame alone was not enough: every woman here is attached to a change that can be pointed to, dated and sourced.

The selection deliberately spans very different routes to consequence — elected power, scientific discovery, civil disobedience, humanitarian work, art, media ownership and sport — and two centuries of birth years, from Marie Curie in 1867 to Malala Yousafzai in 1997. Eight of the fifteen are living. Any list of fifteen also leaves out women who could anchor another: Ada Lovelace, Simone de Beauvoir, Wangari Maathai, Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Kalpana Chawla among them. Their absence is a limit of the format, not a judgement.

The Trailblazers

Six women whose influence was established in the twentieth century — in laboratories, cockpits, buses, studios, prime ministers' offices and the streets of Calcutta.

1. Marie Curie

Field: Physics and chemistry | Base: Paris, France (born in Warsaw, Poland) | Lived: 1867–1934

Quick highlights:

  • Coined the term 'radioactivity' and, with Pierre Curie, discovered the elements polonium and radium
  • Won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911 — still the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
  • Became the first woman professor at the Sorbonne, in 1906

Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, then under Russian rule, Marie Curie moved to Paris to study and built her career in a basement laboratory with her husband Pierre. Their work on the radiation coming from uranium ores — a phenomenon she named radioactivity — produced two new elements, polonium (named for her occupied homeland) and radium, and founded an entirely new branch of science. The Nobel Prizes followed, in Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911, and after Pierre's death she took his chair at the Sorbonne, the university's first woman professor. During the First World War she equipped mobile X-ray units — the 'petites Curies' — that brought imaging to field hospitals. She died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, a condition linked to her years of exposure to radiation.

Why she matters: Curie did not just contribute to science; she created a field, then proved a woman could lead it — winning its highest honour twice, in two different disciplines, at a time when women were largely barred from its institutions.

2. Amelia Earhart

Field: Aviation | Base: United States | Lived: 1897–1937

Quick highlights:

  • In May 1932 became the first woman to fly solo and nonstop across the Atlantic
  • Set a string of women's speed and altitude records through the 1920s and 1930s
  • Co-founded The Ninety-Nines, the organisation of women pilots, in 1929

Amelia Earhart, from Atchison, Kansas, worked as a nurse's aide and social worker before flying consumed her. In 1928 she became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air — as a passenger, a qualification she was always honest about — and in May 1932 she did it again alone, flying nonstop from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in just under fifteen hours. More records followed, and she used her fame deliberately: lecturing, writing and helping to found The Ninety-Nines so that the growing number of women pilots had an institution of their own. In 1937 she set out to fly around the world with navigator Fred Noonan. Her Lockheed Electra disappeared over the Pacific near Howland Island on 2 July 1937; neither the aircraft nor its crew was ever conclusively found.

Why she matters: Earhart's records were real, but her larger influence was demonstrative: in an era when aviation symbolised the future, the most famous pilot in the world was a woman, and she spent that fame opening the field to others.

3. Rosa Parks

Field: Civil rights | Base: Montgomery, Alabama, United States | Lived: 1913–2005

Quick highlights:

  • Her arrest on 1 December 1955, for refusing to surrender her bus seat, sparked the Montgomery bus boycott
  • The boycott lasted 381 days and ended after the US Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional
  • Was secretary of the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP long before she became famous

Rosa Parks was a seamstress in Montgomery, Alabama — and, for more than a decade before her famous arrest, a committed civil rights worker who served as secretary of the local NAACP chapter and investigated racial violence. On 1 December 1955 she refused a bus driver's order to give up her seat to a white passenger and was arrested. Her case became the rallying point for a boycott of Montgomery's buses by the city's Black community, sustained for 381 days under the leadership of a young Martin Luther King Jr., until the Supreme Court's ruling in Browder v. Gayle ended segregation on the city's buses. She later wrote that she was not physically tired that day — she was, in her words, tired of giving in. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1996, and on her death in 2005 became the first woman to lie in honour in the US Capitol rotunda.

Why she matters: Parks turned one person's refusal into a mass movement's founding story — and her years of unglamorous organising before and after 1955 are the real template of how such moments are made.

4. Frida Kahlo

Field: Art | Base: Coyoacán, Mexico City, Mexico | Lived: 1907–1954

Quick highlights:

  • Began painting in earnest while recovering from a devastating bus crash in 1925
  • In 1939 the Louvre bought her painting The Frame — the first work by a Mexican artist to enter its collection
  • Her house, La Casa Azul, is now the Frida Kahlo Museum; her global fame grew enormously after her death

Frida Kahlo's art grew out of physical catastrophe: at eighteen, the bus she was riding in was struck by a tram, fracturing her spine and pelvis and beginning a lifetime of pain and surgeries. Confined to bed for months, she began to paint, often herself — of her 143 paintings, 55 are self-portraits. Works such as The Two Fridas (1939) fused Mexican folk imagery, Catholic iconography and unflinching depictions of her own injured body. Though the Surrealists claimed her, she resisted the label, saying she painted her own reality, not dreams. In her lifetime she was better known internationally as the wife of muralist Diego Rivera; the scale of her reputation today — among the most recognisable artists of the twentieth century, and a symbol of Mexican identity and of living with disability — was built after her death in 1954.

Why she matters: Kahlo made the self-portrait a record of pain, culture and defiance, and her posthumous rise redrew the canon: a disabled Mexican woman, working outside the European mainstream, is now one of its central figures.

5. Indira Gandhi

Field: Politics | Role: Prime Minister of India, 1966–1977 and 1980–1984 | Lived: 1917–1984

Quick highlights:

  • India's first — and so far only — woman Prime Minister, leading the country for fifteen years in total
  • Led India during the 1971 war, after which Bangladesh became an independent country
  • Daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister; assassinated in office in 1984

Indira Gandhi grew up inside India's freedom movement as the daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, and entered the prime minister's office in 1966, two years after his death. She proved a formidable political operator: she nationalised India's major banks in 1969, and in 1971 led the country through a war with Pakistan that ended with the creation of Bangladesh. Her premiership also contains the Emergency of 1975–77, when civil liberties were suspended and opponents jailed — a period she ended by calling elections in 1977, which she lost. Returned to power in 1980, she ordered the army operation at Amritsar's Golden Temple in June 1984 and was assassinated by two of her own bodyguards that October. Her legacy — centraliser, moderniser, and the only woman to have led the world's largest democracy — remains actively debated in India.

Why she matters: Gandhi demonstrated, at the head of a vast and fractious democracy, that a woman could hold and wield supreme executive power for a decade and a half — and her career still frames Indian arguments about strong leadership itself.

6. Mother Teresa

Field: Humanitarian work | Base: Kolkata, India | Lived: 1910–1997

Quick highlights:

  • Founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata in 1950 to serve 'the poorest of the poor'
  • Received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and India's Bharat Ratna in 1980
  • Canonised by the Catholic Church in 2016 as Saint Teresa of Calcutta

Born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu to an Albanian family in Skopje, she joined the Sisters of Loreto and arrived in India in 1929, teaching at a convent school in Calcutta. In 1946, on a train journey, she experienced what she called a 'call within a call' to live among the poor, and in 1950 founded the Missionaries of Charity — beginning with thirteen members and growing, by her death, into an order of thousands working in more than a hundred countries. Her Nirmal Hriday home, opened in 1952, took in the dying from Calcutta's streets. The work brought her the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and worldwide fame, alongside public debate about the standards of care in her homes and her religious conservatism. She died in 1997 and was canonised by Pope Francis in 2016.

Why she matters: Whatever the debates around her methods, Mother Teresa made the destitute of one city's streets a global moral reference point, and built a religious order whose work among the poorest outlived her on every continent.

The Modern Era

Nine women whose influence belongs to the last four decades — chancellors and commission presidents, a vice president, a laureate who began as a schoolgirl blogger, and the finance minister of the world's most populous country.

7. Jane Goodall

Field: Primatology and conservation | Base: Gombe, Tanzania (born in London, United Kingdom) | Lived: 1934–2025

Quick highlights:

  • Began observing wild chimpanzees at Gombe, Tanzania, in 1960 — the study she started still continues today
  • Documented chimpanzees making and using tools, overturning the definition of humans as the only toolmakers
  • Founded the Jane Goodall Institute in 1977 and the Roots & Shoots youth programme in 1991

Jane Goodall arrived at the Gombe Stream reserve in Tanzania in 1960, aged twenty-six, with no university degree — sent by the anthropologist Louis Leakey precisely because her mind was uncluttered by theory. By patiently winning the chimpanzees' tolerance, she observed what science had not: chimpanzees fashioning tools to fish for termites, eating meat, and living in societies of intricate relationships and occasional violence. The findings forced a redefinition of what separates humans from other animals, and the study she founded became the longest-running research project on wild primates. From the 1980s she turned increasingly to advocacy, founding the Jane Goodall Institute in 1977 and Roots & Shoots in 1991, and was named a UN Messenger of Peace in 2002. She was still travelling and speaking in her nineties, and died on a speaking tour in Los Angeles on 1 October 2025, aged 91.

Why she matters: Goodall changed the science of animal behaviour from inside a forest clearing, then spent a second career — longer than the first — converting that authority into a worldwide conservation movement.

8. Angela Merkel

Field: Politics | Role: Chancellor of Germany, 2005–2021 | Born: 1954

Quick highlights:

  • Chancellor of Germany for sixteen years (2005–2021) — the first woman to hold the office
  • Led Germany through the financial crisis, the euro crisis, the 2015 migration crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic
  • Ranked by Forbes as the world's most powerful woman for ten years in a row; published her memoir, Freedom, in 2024

Angela Merkel was a research physicist in communist East Germany when the Berlin Wall fell in 1989; within a year she was in politics, and by 2000 she led the Christian Democratic Union. In November 2005 she became Chancellor of Germany — the first woman, and the first East German, to hold the post. Her sixteen years in office were defined by crisis management: the global financial crash, the eurozone debt crisis, the arrival of more than a million refugees and migrants in 2015–16, met with her phrase 'Wir schaffen das' ('We can do this'), and the pandemic. A style of patient, evidence-led negotiation made her for many the de facto leader of Europe. She chose not to seek a fifth term and left office in December 2021; her memoir Freedom appeared in 2024.

Why she matters: Merkel normalised the idea of a woman leading a major power for a generation of voters — not as an exception to be noted, but as the default statesperson of Europe for sixteen years.

9. Oprah Winfrey

Field: Media and business | Base: United States | Born: 1954

Quick highlights:

  • Hosted The Oprah Winfrey Show for 25 seasons (1986–2011), the defining talk show of its era
  • In 2003 became the first Black woman billionaire, through her company Harpo Productions
  • Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013; her book club repeatedly reshaped bestseller lists

Oprah Winfrey was born into poverty in rural Mississippi and was working in local television while still a teenager. A Chicago morning show she took over in 1984 became, within two years, the nationally syndicated Oprah Winfrey Show, whose confessional, bookish, self-examining style ran for twenty-five seasons and made her the most influential interviewer in America. She kept ownership of the programme through her company Harpo — the foundation of a fortune that in 2003 made her, by Forbes' reckoning, the first Black woman billionaire. Oprah's Book Club could turn a novel into a phenomenon overnight; her leadership academy for girls in South Africa opened in 2007; her endorsement in the 2008 US presidential race was treated as a political event in itself. She launched the OWN network in 2011 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.

Why she matters: Winfrey's influence is a template of its own: she converted a television audience into cultural authority — over what America read, discussed and, at times, voted for — while owning the means of production herself.

10. Serena Williams

Field: Sport (tennis) | Base: United States | Born: 1981

Quick highlights:

  • Won 23 Grand Slam singles titles — the most by any player in the Open Era
  • Won four Olympic gold medals and held all four major titles at once, twice (the 'Serena Slam')
  • Stepped away from tennis after the 2022 US Open; rejoined the sport's anti-doping testing pool in late 2025

Serena Williams, raised in Compton, California, and coached by her father Richard alongside her sister Venus, won her first major at the 1999 US Open at seventeen. Across the next twenty-three years she accumulated 23 Grand Slam singles titles — more than any other player of the Open Era — four Olympic gold medals, and two separate runs holding all four major titles simultaneously. She won the 2017 Australian Open while eight weeks pregnant. In 2022 she wrote that she was 'evolving away' from tennis, and played her last tournament at that year's US Open. Through her firm Serena Ventures she has become a significant investor, and in late 2025 she rejoined tennis's anti-doping testing pool — the formal step that makes a retired player eligible to compete again — while publicly declining to confirm that a comeback is planned.

Why she matters: Williams redrew the physical and commercial possibilities of women's tennis, dominated it across three decades, and then carried the same authority into business — all from a public-court upbringing the sport had never produced a champion from before.

11. Ursula von der Leyen

Field: Politics | Role: President of the European Commission, 2019–present | Born: 1958

Quick highlights:

  • President of the European Commission since December 2019 — the first woman to lead the institution
  • Previously Germany's defence minister (2013–2019), also the first woman in that role
  • Re-elected by the European Parliament in 2024; her second Commission took office on 1 December 2024

Ursula von der Leyen, born in Brussels and trained as a physician, entered German politics through Lower Saxony and became a federal minister under Angela Merkel — serving in the family and labour portfolios before becoming, in 2013, the first woman to lead Germany's defence ministry. In 2019 the European Council nominated her to head the European Commission, and she took office that December — again the first woman in the role. Her first term was dominated by the pandemic, for which the Commission organised joint EU vaccine procurement and a vast common recovery fund, by the completion of Brexit, and by coordinating the EU's response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The European Parliament re-elected her in July 2024, and her second Commission, with a term running to 2029, took office on 1 December 2024, with competitiveness and defence at the top of its programme.

Why she matters: Von der Leyen holds what is arguably the most powerful executive office in the world occupied by a woman today, and her tenure has shifted the Commission toward the geopolitical centre of European decision-making.

12. Kamala Harris

Field: Politics | Role: Vice President of the United States, 2021–2025 | Born: 1964

Quick highlights:

  • Vice President of the United States from 2021 to 2025 — the first woman, first Black American and first person of South Asian descent to hold the office
  • Previously Attorney General of California (2011–2017) and a United States Senator (2017–2021)
  • Became the Democratic presidential nominee in July 2024 and contested that year's election; published the memoir 107 Days in 2025

Kamala Harris, born in Oakland, California, to a Jamaican economist father and an Indian cancer-researcher mother, built her career in prosecution: San Francisco's district attorney, then California's attorney general, then the US Senate. In January 2021 she was sworn in as Vice President — the first woman, and the first Black and South Asian American, to reach the office. When President Joe Biden withdrew from the 2024 election that July, Harris became the Democratic nominee and ran a 107-day campaign, losing in November to Donald Trump. Since leaving office she has lived in California, announced in July 2025 that she would not run for the state's governorship in 2026, and published a memoir of the campaign, 107 Days, that September. She remains an active figure in Democratic politics, campaigning for the party's candidates.

Why she matters: Harris broke three barriers at once in reaching the vice presidency, and her 2024 candidacy — the shortest modern presidential campaign — made her the second woman to head a major US party's ticket, and the closest any has come to the presidency by electoral votes contested.

13. Jacinda Ardern

Field: Politics | Role: Prime Minister of New Zealand, 2017–2023 | Born: 1980

Quick highlights:

  • Became New Zealand's Prime Minister in October 2017, aged 37 — the world's youngest female head of government at the time
  • In 2018 became the second elected head of government in modern history to give birth while in office
  • Led New Zealand through the Christchurch mosque attacks, the Whakaari eruption and the COVID-19 pandemic before resigning in 2023

Jacinda Ardern took over the New Zealand Labour Party seven weeks before the 2017 election and, at thirty-seven, became the country's youngest prime minister in more than 150 years. In June 2018 she gave birth to her daughter while in office — only the second elected head of government in modern times, after Pakistan's Benazir Bhutto, to do so. Her response to the Christchurch mosque attacks of March 2019, in which 51 people were killed — public mourning alongside Muslim communities, and a ban on military-style semi-automatic weapons passed within weeks — drew worldwide attention, as did her government's elimination strategy in the first phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, rewarded with a landslide re-election in 2020. She resigned in January 2023, saying she no longer had 'enough in the tank'. She has since held fellowships at Harvard, published the memoir A Different Kind of Power (2025), and in October 2026 joined the University of Sydney as a Professor of Practice.

Why she matters: Ardern became the global reference case for a different register of leadership — empathy performed as policy, tested through terrorism, disaster and plague — and her example is still argued over wherever that style is proposed or resisted.

14. Malala Yousafzai

Field: Education activism | Base: Pakistan and the United Kingdom | Born: 1997

Quick highlights:

  • Shot by a Taliban gunman in October 2012, aged fifteen, for campaigning for girls' education in Pakistan's Swat Valley
  • Received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014 — at seventeen, the youngest laureate in the prize's history
  • Co-founded the Malala Fund in 2013, which campaigns for girls' secondary education worldwide

Malala Yousafzai grew up in Mingora, in Pakistan's Swat Valley, where her father ran a school. When the Taliban took control of the valley and moved to stop girls attending school, she — aged eleven — began writing an anonymous diary for BBC Urdu about life under their rule, and later spoke publicly for girls' education. On 9 October 2012 a Taliban gunman boarded her school bus and shot her. Flown to Britain for treatment, she recovered, and on her sixteenth birthday addressed the United Nations. The Malala Fund, co-founded with her father in 2013, campaigns and raises money for girls' schooling in countries from Pakistan to Nigeria and Brazil. In 2014 she received the Nobel Peace Prize jointly with India's Kailash Satyarthi, becoming, at seventeen, its youngest-ever laureate. She later studied at the University of Oxford, graduating in 2020, and continues her advocacy.

Why she matters: Malala's influence began with a schoolgirl's diary and survived an assassin's bullet: she converted personal survival into the most recognisable global campaign for girls' education, and remains its face a decade on.

15. Nirmala Sitharaman

Field: Politics and public finance | Role: Minister of Finance of India, 2019–present | Born: 1959

Quick highlights:

  • India's Minister of Finance and Corporate Affairs since May 2019 — the first woman to hold the finance portfolio full-time
  • Presented her ninth consecutive Union Budget in February 2026, a record run
  • Previously served as Defence Minister (2017–2019)

Nirmala Sitharaman, from Madurai in Tamil Nadu, worked in London and then in research and party politics in India before entering the Union Council of Ministers in 2014 as a commerce minister. In September 2017 she became Defence Minister — only the second woman to hold the post, after Indira Gandhi, who had held it alongside the premiership. In May 2019 she moved to finance, becoming the first woman to hold that portfolio on a full-time basis. She has presented the Union Budget every year since — a ninth consecutive presentation in February 2026, a record streak — steering the presentation of budgets through the pandemic contraction and the recovery that followed. As finance minister she also chairs the GST Council, the federal body that sets India's goods and services tax rates.

Why she matters: Sitharaman holds the economic levers of the world's most populous country, and her unbroken run of budgets is itself a record: no Indian finance minister — man or woman — has presented so many in succession.

What Connects Them

Read together, the fifteen careers share a pattern that is more useful than any ranking. Almost none of them inherited a clear path: Curie worked in a shed, Parks organised for a decade before her famous afternoon, Earhart was a social worker, Winfrey a teenage newsreader, Yousafzai a schoolgirl with a diary. In each case the influence came from converting an unpromising position into an institution — a science, a movement, an order, a company, a fund, a record book — that continued after them.

The second pattern is resistance met and priced in. The women on this list were shot at, arrested, assassinated, exiled from their professions or dismissed as novelties, and the record of how they responded is much of why they are remembered. Influence, in these fifteen cases at least, was rarely granted. It was taken, documented, and then defended long enough to become history.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the most influential woman in history?
There is no official answer — influence cannot be measured like a race. The names most consistently cited by historians and encyclopaedias include Marie Curie, whose work founded a science, and figures such as Rosa Parks and Mother Teresa, whose actions and institutions reached far beyond their own countries. This list presents fifteen of the strongest cases and explains each.

Is this list a ranking?
No. It is an editorial selection, ordered broadly by era — trailblazers first, then the modern period — rather than by merit. No official body ranks historical influence, and we have not invented one.

How many of the women on the list are still living?
Eight of the fifteen, as of October 2026: Angela Merkel, Oprah Winfrey, Serena Williams, Ursula von der Leyen, Kamala Harris, Jacinda Ardern, Malala Yousafzai and Nirmala Sitharaman. Jane Goodall, the most recently deceased, died on 1 October 2025.

Who is the youngest person on the list?
Malala Yousafzai, born in 1997. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014 at the age of seventeen — still the youngest laureate in the prize's history.

How were the photographs chosen?
Each image is a real photograph of the woman herself, sourced from Wikimedia Commons and checked twice — against the file's own description and by visual inspection. Two file-page traps were rejected during research, including a photograph labelled with a European leader's name that actually pictures a different politician. Full credits are in the research note below.

Conclusion

Fifteen lives, fifteen different mechanisms of consequence: a laboratory, a cockpit, a bus seat, a sickbed easel, a prime minister's desk, a hospice, a forest clearing, a chancellery, a television studio, a tennis court, a commission, a campaign, a classroom cause and a finance ministry. If this list has a single lesson, it is that influence is not a personality trait — it is what remains when documented work outlasts the person who did it.

Research note: Biographical details were compiled in October 2026 from reputable published references, including Encyclopaedia Britannica entries, official institutional biographies (the Nobel Prize organisation, the European Commission, the Jane Goodall Institute, the Press Information Bureau of India) and broadsheet reporting, and current offices were re-verified at the time of writing. Photographs are real photographs of each woman from Wikimedia Commons, identity-checked against the file records: Marie Curie (Henri Manuel, public domain); Amelia Earhart (Smithsonian Institution, public domain); Rosa Parks (Gene Herrick for the Associated Press, 1956, public domain); Frida Kahlo (Guillermo Kahlo, 1932, public domain); Indira Gandhi (Prime Minister's Office, GODL-India); Mother Teresa (Túrelio, 1986, CC BY-SA 2.0 DE); Jane Goodall (Franz Johann Morgenbesser, 2015, CC BY-SA 2.0 — cropped from the original award photograph); Angela Merkel (Kristof Roomp, 2019, CC0); Oprah Winfrey (aphrodite-in-nyc, 2014, CC BY 2.0); Serena Williams (Paulobrad, 2012, CC BY-SA 4.0); Ursula von der Leyen (Dati Bendo, European Union, 2023, CC BY 4.0 — cropped to the subject from the original press-conference photograph); Kamala Harris (Lawrence Jackson, White House, 2021, public domain); Jacinda Ardern (Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, New Zealand, 2019, CC BY 4.0); Malala Yousafzai (DFID, 2015, CC BY 2.0); Nirmala Sitharaman (Ministry of Finance, Government of India, 2023, GODL-India). The cover compiles the photographs of Marie Curie, Rosa Parks, Kamala Harris and Malala Yousafzai. This is an editorial selection, not an official ranking.

Each with a verified photograph, the achievement she is known for, and why it mattered. An editorial selection, not an official ranking.

title.rendered: Sidhu Moose Wala Murder Case: What Happened, What Police Allege, and Where the Case Stands

content.rendered:
Quick answer: Punjabi singer Sidhu Moose Wala — real name Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu — was shot dead on 29 May 2022 near Jawaharke village in Punjab's Mansa district, a day after his police security cover was reduced. Within hours, Canada-based gangster Goldy Brar claimed responsibility for the killing. Punjab Police allege the murder was planned by Brar with jailed gangster Lawrence Bishnoi, whom the police chargesheet names as the mastermind. More than four years on, the trial is still under way in a Mansa court and no accused has been convicted. This explainer separates what is established fact, what the police and prosecution allege, and what the accused have claimed — and gives the case's status as of October 2026.

A note on how to read this article, because it matters in an unfinished court case. Statements marked as fact are drawn from reputable reporting of the court record, official statements and the post-mortem findings reported at the time. Statements introduced with "police allege", "according to the chargesheet" or "prosecutors say" are allegations that the prosecution must still prove in court; every person in custody is an accused, not a convict, and is presumed innocent until a court decides otherwise. Statements by Goldy Brar are his own claims, reported because he is a central figure in the case, not because they are accepted as true.

Who Sidhu Moose Wala Was

Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu (11 June 1993 – 29 May 2022) | Moosa village, Mansa district, Punjab | Singer, songwriter and actor; Congress candidate from Mansa in the 2022 Punjab Assembly election

Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu was born on 11 June 1993 in Moosa, a village in Punjab's Mansa district, the only child of Balkaur Singh and Charan Kaur. He took his stage name from the village itself — "Moose Wala" means "the one from Moosa" — and returned to live there even after he became famous, building a house that fans still visit. He studied electrical engineering at Guru Nanak Dev Engineering College in Ludhiana, graduating in 2016, and then moved to Canada as an international student, settling in Brampton, Ontario.

His music career began as a songwriter: the first song he wrote, "License", was recorded by the singer Ninja. His own singing started with a duet, "G Wagon", recorded while he was in Canada, but the breakthrough came in 2017 with "So High", a collaboration with producer Byg Byrd that won him the Best Lyricist award at the Brit Asia TV Music Awards. His debut album, PBX 1 (2018), reached the Billboard Canadian Albums chart, and his single "47" entered the UK Singles Chart. In 2020, The Guardian named him among its 50 new artists to watch. His third album, Moosetape (2021), anchored by tracks such as "295", charted internationally and confirmed him as the most commercially successful Punjabi artist of his generation — an artist from a farming village whose songs about rural pride, family and defiance were streamed hundreds of millions of times across India and the Punjabi diaspora. He also founded his own label and acted in Punjabi films, including Moosa Jatt and Yes I Am Student.

His career was not without controversy, and a factual account should say so plainly. His lyrics frequently referenced guns and gang rivalry, and critics — including within Punjab — accused him of glamorising gun culture; he and his supporters countered that he was describing the world he came from. In 2020 he was booked under the Arms Act after a video of him firing an AK-47 at a shooting range during the Covid lockdown went viral, an episode reported widely at the time. None of that history is an explanation for his murder; it is context for the public argument that followed it.

In December 2021 he joined the Indian National Congress and contested the 2022 Punjab Assembly election from Mansa. He lost to the Aam Aadmi Party's Dr Vijay Singla. By the spring of 2022 he was back in Punjab, recording, campaigning on local issues and, according to his father Balkaur Singh's statement to police, receiving extortion and threat calls from gangsters, including from the Lawrence Bishnoi gang — a claim recorded in the First Information Report (FIR) registered on his father's complaint after the murder, as reported by The Indian Express.

What Happened on 29 May 2022

On 28 May 2022, the Punjab Police scaled back the security cover of 424 protectees across the state, a step the government presented as a temporary, routine exercise ahead of the anniversary of Operation Blue Star. Moose Wala was among them: his detail was reduced from four police personnel to two, according to contemporary reporting. Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann later ordered an inquiry into why the cover had been pruned.

On the afternoon of Sunday, 29 May 2022, Moose Wala left his home in Moosa in his Mahindra Thar, driving to Jawaharke village, about ten kilometres away, to visit relatives. With him were his cousin Gurvinder Singh and his friend Gurpreet Singh. He did not take the two remaining security personnel with him, and he was not travelling in his bulletproof vehicle. According to the FIR, registered on his father's complaint, Balkaur Singh followed in a second vehicle with the gunmen because of the threat calls his son had been receiving.

Near Jawaharke, the Thar was intercepted by two vehicles, one of them a white Bolero. Police say six shooters, working in two modules, opened fire on the vehicle. Gurvinder Singh and Gurpreet Singh were injured. Moose Wala was rushed to the Civil Hospital in Mansa, where he was declared dead. He was 28. Reporting at the time, citing the autopsy, recorded 19 bullet injury marks on his body. News of the killing — in broad daylight, a day after his security was reduced — caused shock across Punjab and among Punjabi communities worldwide. Chief Minister Mann, who called the singer "a cultural icon of Punjab", ordered a high-level inquiry into the security lapse alongside the murder investigation.

The Claim of Responsibility, and What Police Allege

Within hours of the shooting, a post on Facebook in the name of Goldy Brar claimed responsibility for the murder on behalf of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. Brar — real name Satinderjit Singh, a native of Sri Muktsar Sahib who had gone to Canada on a student visa in 2017 — is described by police as a close associate of Lawrence Bishnoi, the gang leader who has been in jail for years in a series of cases. The claim, as reported by Punjab Police, said the killing was retaliation for the murder of Youth Akali Dal leader Vicky Middukhera, who was shot dead in Mohali in August 2021. Punjab's Director General of Police, VK Bhawra, told the media the same day that the Bishnoi gang was behind the killing and that it appeared to be the result of inter-gang rivalry.

Two cautions belong here. First, the gang's assertion that people around Moose Wala were involved in the Middukhera murder has never been established in court, and Moose Wala himself was never charged in that case. Second, everything in this section and the next is the prosecution's case or the gang's own claims — none of it has yet been tested to a verdict.

According to the police chargesheet, summarised in later court reporting, the murder was planned by Goldy Brar in coordination with Lawrence Bishnoi, Jaggu Bhagwanpuria and others, and carried out to avenge Middukhera's killing; the chargesheet names Bishnoi as the mastermind. Hindustan Times has reported that both investigators and Brar himself trace a key trigger to a kabaddi tournament at Bhago Majra village in February 2020, organised by youths linked to the rival Bambiha gang, which Moose Wala promoted despite, police say, a warning from Bishnoi to stay away. In June 2025, in an audio interview for the BBC World Service documentary The Killing Call, Brar again said that he had ordered the killing, claiming the singer had "made some mistakes that could not be forgiven" and alleging that Moose Wala had helped the gang's rivals. Those are Brar's claims, made while he remains a fugitive accused in the case; they are recorded here because he made them publicly, not as findings of fact.

The Investigation: Arrests, an Encounter and the Chargesheet

The Punjab government set up a Special Investigation Team for the case, headed by the chief of the Anti-Gangster Task Force, Pramod Ban. The investigation that followed was one of the largest in the state's recent history. Its main milestones, as reported, were:

  • June–July 2022: The Special Cell of the Delhi Police arrested four of the men police identify as shooters — Priyavrat Fauji and Kashish, and then Ankit Sirsa and Sachin Bhiwani.
  • 20 July 2022: Two more identified shooters, Jagroop Singh Roopa and Manpreet Singh "Mannu" Kussa, were killed in an encounter with Punjab Police near Bhakna village in Amritsar district, close to the Pakistan border, where police said they had taken shelter in an abandoned building.
  • 10 September 2022: The sixth and last identified shooter, Deepak "Mundi", was arrested with two associates, Kapil Pandit and Rajinder, near the West Bengal–Nepal border in a joint operation by the Anti-Gangster Task Force, central agencies and Delhi Police, Punjab DGP Gaurav Yadav announced. With that arrest, police said, all six shooters named in the case had been accounted for.
  • 26 February 2023: Two accused in the case, Mandeep Singh "Toofan" and Manmohan Singh "Mohana", were killed in a clash between rival gang groups inside Goindwal Sahib Central Jail in Tarn Taran district; seven inmates were booked over the killings, according to PTI reporting at the time.
  • 1 August 2023: Sachin Bishnoi, also known as Sachin Thapan — named in the chargesheet as an accused who had fled India on a forged passport before the murder and had, police said, helped with logistics — was extradited from Azerbaijan, where he had been detained in Baku in August 2022, and brought to Delhi by the Special Cell.

On 26 August 2022, just inside the 90-day deadline, Mansa police filed the first chargesheet in the case: 1,850 pages, against 24 people, with 122 witnesses, as The Tribune and The Indian Express reported. The FIR in the case named 36 people in total. Of the 24 in the first chargesheet, 20 were in custody — including Lawrence Bishnoi, named by police as the mastermind, and Jaggu Bhagwanpuria — and four were absconding abroad: Goldy Brar, Sachin Thapan, Anmol Bishnoi (Lawrence Bishnoi's younger brother) and Lipin Nehra. Supplementary chargesheets followed, and the prosecution's witness list has since grown to about 180.

Where the Case Stands — as of October 2026

The trial is under way, and there has been no conviction. On 1 May 2024, the court of the District and Sessions Judge in Mansa framed charges against 27 accused, including Lawrence Bishnoi and Jaggu Bhagwanpuria, under sections of the Indian Penal Code including 302 (murder), 307 (attempt to murder) and 120-B (criminal conspiracy), along with provisions of the Arms Act and the Prisons Act. The court dismissed discharge applications by Bishnoi and three other accused. Charges could not be framed against Goldy Brar: he has never been arrested or produced before the court, a position that remains unchanged as of October 2026.

Since then, the case has been at the evidence stage, moving slowly. The prosecution's list runs to roughly 180 witnesses. At a bail hearing in September 2026, the defence pointed out that only 20 of them had been examined, The Indian Express reported; the prosecution, for its part, told the Supreme Court in March 2026 that protected witnesses had already testified. Moose Wala's father, Balkaur Singh, is the complainant in the case and one of its principal witnesses. Two recent court developments show the pattern of the litigation:

  • March 2026: The Supreme Court granted bail to two accused, Pawan Bishnoi and Jagtar Singh, who had spent more than three and a half years in custody, after argument centred on the slow pace of the trial and the number of witnesses still to be heard. Bail is not an acquittal: both men remain accused and continue to face the trial.
  • September 2026: The Punjab and Haryana High Court dismissed the bail plea of another accused, Joginder Singh alias Joga, holding — on the prosecution's material, which alleges he sheltered the shooters and supplied a weapon — that he was "one of the prime conspirators", and noting the risk to eyewitnesses if he were released. That is a bail-stage assessment of the allegations, not a verdict.

As for the two best-known names outside the courtroom: Goldy Brar remains a fugitive. An Interpol Red Corner Notice was issued against him after the murder. In December 2022, Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann announced that Brar had been detained in California; the Indian Express has since reported that this announcement later proved incorrect. In January 2024, the Union Home Ministry designated Brar a terrorist under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. In September 2026, the Indian Express reported that the US Federal Bureau of Investigation had added Brar to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, with a reward of one million dollars for information leading to his capture — an announcement Punjab Police publicly welcomed. Anmol Bishnoi, named as an absconding accused in the Moose Wala chargesheet, was deported from the United States and arrested on arrival in Delhi on 19 November 2025 by the National Investigation Agency — in the NIA's separate case concerning an alleged terror-gangster network, in which he had been chargesheeted in 2023. He is lodged in Tihar Jail, and a government order restricting his removal from prison currently limits how other agencies and courts can obtain his production.

The honest summary, as of October 2026, is this: the shooters identified by police have been arrested or are dead; the alleged organisers are in custody in India or, in Brar's case, still sought abroad; the charges have been framed and evidence is being recorded — but more than four years after the murder, no court has yet delivered a verdict on who was responsible.

His Family's Fight for Justice

The case exists because Moose Wala's father pursued it from the first hour. The FIR was registered on Balkaur Singh's complaint; in it, he described following his son's vehicle with the remaining gunmen and reaching the scene of the shooting. On 4 June 2022, Balkaur Singh and Charan Kaur met Union Home Minister Amit Shah at Chandigarh airport and demanded that a central agency investigate the murder; the investigation nonetheless remained with the Punjab Police, whose chief minister assured the family that the killers would be caught. On 25 August 2022, the parents led a candle march from their home to Jawaharke, the village where their son was killed. In December 2022, Balkaur Singh publicly offered to fund a reward of ₹2 crore from his own pocket for information leading to Goldy Brar's arrest, as reported at the time.

When charges were framed in May 2024, Balkaur Singh — who attends the proceedings — said the family felt "some relief" for the first time in two years, and that they had full faith in the judiciary but wanted regular hearings and speedy justice. The family has also resisted portrayals of their son that they did not approve. In June 2025, Balkaur Singh petitioned a Mansa court to stop the screening of the BBC World Service documentary The Killing Call, arguing that the family had not consented to it and that it could affect the ongoing trial; the court declined to grant an interim stay, and the BBC released the two-part film on YouTube on 11 June 2025, Moose Wala's birth anniversary. The family's position, stated repeatedly in public, is that nothing — money, films or anniversaries — substitutes for a verdict.

Legacy

Moose Wala's music has continued to reach audiences after his death. His song "SYL", about the Sutlej–Yamuna Link canal dispute, was released posthumously on 23 June 2022; it was later blocked in India following a legal complaint. Further recordings made before his death have been released by his estate, among them "Mera Na" (2023), a collaboration with the Nigerian singer Burna Boy and the British producer Steel Banglez. His songs — above all "295" and "The Last Ride", the latter released in the final weeks of his life — remain fixtures of Punjabi playlists, and his home in Moosa draws a steady stream of visitors.

His murder also changed the conversation around him. It forced a public reckoning in Punjab with the extortion threats that police dossiers describe as routinely directed at singers, actors and businessmen by gang networks operating from abroad; with the practice of reducing or withdrawing police protection; and with the way fame in the Punjabi music industry had become entangled, at its edges, with organised crime. Those are debates, not verdicts. The verdict in his own case is still awaited.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Sidhu Moose Wala?
Sidhu Moose Wala (born Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu, 11 June 1993) was a Punjabi singer, rapper, songwriter and actor from Moosa village in Punjab's Mansa district. He rose from writing songs for other artists to becoming the most commercially successful Punjabi artist of his generation, with albums including PBX 1 and Moosetape, before entering politics as a Congress candidate in the 2022 Punjab Assembly election.

When and where was Sidhu Moose Wala killed?
He was shot on 29 May 2022 near Jawaharke village in Mansa district, Punjab, while travelling in his Mahindra Thar with his cousin and a friend, who were injured. He was declared dead at the Civil Hospital in Mansa. He was 28 years old.

Who claimed responsibility for the murder?
Canada-based gangster Goldy Brar claimed responsibility in a Facebook post made within hours of the killing, and repeated the claim in a 2025 BBC interview. A claim is not proof: Punjab Police have built their own case, set out in chargesheets, and it is that case which is now being tested at trial.

Who do police allege organised the murder?
According to the chargesheet, the murder was planned by Goldy Brar in coordination with Lawrence Bishnoi, Jaggu Bhagwanpuria and others, and the police chargesheet names Lawrence Bishnoi as the mastermind. Police allege the motive was revenge for the August 2021 murder of Youth Akali Dal leader Vicky Middukhera. These are allegations; the accused are entitled to the presumption of innocence, and no court has yet ruled on them.

Has anyone been convicted?
No. As of October 2026, the trial is at the evidence stage in the Mansa sessions court. Charges were framed against 27 accused in May 2024; of the roughly 180 prosecution witnesses, only a fraction had been examined by September 2026, as the defence noted in a bail hearing. Some accused have been granted bail during the long trial, which is not the same as being acquitted.

Where is Goldy Brar?
He has never been arrested in this case and charges have not been framed against him because he has not been produced before the court. He was designated a terrorist under the UAPA in January 2024, and in September 2026 the Indian Express reported that the FBI had placed him on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list with a one-million-dollar reward. A December 2022 announcement by Punjab's chief minister that Brar had been detained in California later proved incorrect.

Why was Moose Wala's security reduced the day before he was killed?
On 28 May 2022, Punjab Police scaled back the security of 424 protectees in what the state government described as a temporary exercise ahead of the anniversary of Operation Blue Star; Moose Wala's detail was reduced from four personnel to two. On the day of the attack he travelled without the two remaining personnel. Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann ordered an inquiry into the pruning decision.

Conclusion

The murder of Sidhu Moose Wala is, at once, a family's loss, a landmark Punjabi cultural event, and an unfinished criminal case. What happened on 29 May 2022 is known in outline and confirmed by the court record so far: a 28-year-old singer, a day after his security was reduced, was ambushed near his home village and killed. Who bears criminal responsibility for organising it is a question that, as of October 2026, remains where it belongs — before a court in Mansa, still hearing evidence. This page will be updated when that court gives its answer.

Research note: This explainer was compiled in October 2026 from reputable published reporting, principally The Indian Express, The Tribune, Hindustan Times, The Hindu and PTI wire reporting carried by national outlets, including court reporting of September 2026 and the Indian Express's report of 29 September 2026 on the FBI listing. Allegations are attributed throughout to the police, the chargesheet, the prosecution or the person making them; nothing in this article should be read as a finding of guilt against any accused person. Case status is stated as of October 2026. Photographs are real photographs of Sidhu Moose Wala from Wikimedia Commons, identity-checked against the file records and visually: Moosa Jatt shoot and portrait (Shekha Gill, CC BY-SA 4.0); interview at Moosa, 2022 (5911Media, CC BY-SA 4.0); interview, 2019 (Bollywood Tadka / Punjabi Fever, CC BY 3.0). No photographs of any accused person, and no crime-scene images, are used.

excerpt.rendered: Punjabi singer Sidhu Moose Wala was shot dead near Jawaharke village in Punjab’s Mansa district on 29 May 2022, a day after his security cover was reduced. Goldy Brar claimed responsibility; Punjab Police allege Lawrence Bishnoi masterminded the killing. A factual explainer: what happened, what is alleged, and where the trial stands as of October 2026.

title.rendered: Top Jewellers in India: 13 Leading Jewellery Brands Profiled (2026)

content.rendered:
Quick answer first, then the detailed list — 13 of India's leading jewellery retailers, each with its headquarters, founding year and what it is actually known for. This is an editorial selection by VisitBest, not an official ranking: India has lakhs of jewellery businesses, most of them single-store family firms, and no authority publishes a single league table of them. Where a company publishes its own logo, we show it; where its website would not release one to us, the company is described in words instead — never illustrated with a stock picture or another firm's image.

Gold jewellery in India is not really a fashion purchase. It is wedding infrastructure, family savings and festival ritual rolled into one, bought in a market that industry bodies such as the India Brand Equity Foundation (IBEF) routinely describe as one of the largest in the world. For most of history that market belonged to the family jeweller — one store, one lane, trust built over generations. The 13 names in this guide are the businesses that scaled beyond that model: century-old houses, regional giants that own their home states, and national chains run as modern retail. What separates them from the family store is not necessarily better gold — hallmarking law now governs everyone — but systems: published prices, written buy-back policies, and the same experience in every city.

Read the profiles for the story of each house, and keep the buying guide near the end open when you actually shop: it explains BIS hallmarking, the HUID code, making charges and buy-back terms in plain language, because those four things decide what your jewellery is really worth far more than which logo is on the showroom.

Quick Answer: Which Jewellers Should You Look at First?

For a standardised national experience, start with Tanishq and Reliance Jewels. For sheer wedding range in the south and the Gulf, look at Kalyan Jewellers, Malabar Gold & Diamonds and Joyalukkas. For regional mastery, it is GRT Jewellers for Tamil bridal and temple work, Senco for Bengali handcrafted gold, Waman Hari Pethe and TBZ for Maharashtrian weddings, and Bhima, Jos Alukkas and Khazana in their southern heartlands. PC Jeweller is the northern large-format name, currently rebuilding after a difficult decade. The full profiles explain what each house actually does.

How India's Jewellery Market Is Organised

Three layers coexist. At the base are the family jewellers — still the majority of the trade by store count — whose offer is personal trust and credit relationships, and whose gold is now subject to the same mandatory BIS hallmarking as everyone else's. Above them sit the regional chains in this list's middle: houses like GRT, Senco, Bhima and WHP that grew from one city's wedding market into dominance across a state or a cultural region, and whose design libraries reflect that region's traditions — temple jewellery in Tamil Nadu, filigree-light handcrafted work in Bengal, the thushi and mohanmala in Maharashtra, heavy bridal sets in Kerala. At the top are the national and corporate players — Titan's Tanishq, Reliance Jewels, and the Kerala-born chains Kalyan, Malabar and Joyalukkas that expanded across India and the Gulf.

Two forces keep pushing buyers up those layers. The first is regulation: hallmarking with a traceable HUID code has made purity a verifiable fact rather than a promise, which plays to organised retailers' strengths. The second is the wedding itself — a multi-day, multi-outfit event in which families buy for the bride, the groom and the extended family in a single season, and prefer one roof where they can compare a region's full range. None of this makes the family jeweller obsolete; it means the chains in this guide win on range, systems and paperwork, and it is on paperwork that you should judge them.

Top Jewellers in India — Quick Comparison

Detailed Profiles: 13 Leading Jewellers in India

1. Tanishq (Titan Company)

Headquarters: Bengaluru, Karnataka  |  Founded: 1994 (first store 1996)  |  Focus: Bridal and everyday gold and diamond jewellery

Quick highlights:

  • The jewellery division of Titan Company, the Tata Group company promoted with TIDCO; the brand dates to 1994 and its first store opened in 1996
  • Brought organised retail practices to the trade, including the in-store Karatmeter, an X-ray purity tester introduced to check the gold customers already owned
  • Runs sub-brands including Mia, its lightweight line for working women launched in 2011, and Zoya, its luxury diamond label

Tanishq is the name that taught urban India to buy gold jewellery the way it buys everything else — from a branded showroom, at a printed price, with purity stated up front. Titan launched the brand as an export venture, pivoted it to Indian consumers in the mid-1990s, and nearly lost the bet by opening with 18-karat gold; Indian buyers, who treat gold as savings as much as adornment, wanted 22-karat, and the brand corrected course. Its Karatmeter episode is industry folklore: by testing jewellery bought elsewhere and showing customers what they actually owned, Tanishq made transparency its advertising. Today it is the flagship of the largest organised jewellery business in the country, spanning heavy bridal sets, diamond jewellery and lightweight daily-wear lines, with manufacturing anchored at Hosur in Tamil Nadu.

VisitBest recommendation: Start with Tanishq if you want the most standardised buying experience in Indian jewellery — uniform pricing, published policies and a store in almost every large city.

2. Kalyan Jewellers

Headquarters: Thrissur, Kerala  |  Founded: 1993  |  Focus: Large-format showrooms, wedding jewellery and regional collections

Quick highlights:

  • Founded in 1993 in Thrissur by T. S. Kalyanaraman, whose family had run textile businesses in the city for generations
  • Built its name on very large showrooms and on stocking wedding collections matched to each region's traditions, marketed under its Muhurat wedding line
  • Owns Candere, the online-first jewellery brand it acquired in stages between 2017 and 2024; listed on the stock exchanges in 2021

Kalyan's insight was that the Indian jewellery buyer did not want a boutique — she wanted a supermarket of gold. From a single Thrissur showroom in 1993, T. S. Kalyanaraman expanded through Kerala and Tamil Nadu and then across India and the Gulf with big, brightly lit stores carrying deep stock for weddings, which remain the engine of Indian gold demand. The chain localises aggressively: a Kalyan store stocks the bridal sets its own region wears, not a national template. The Gulf showrooms serve the same South Indian customer base abroad. For a buyer, Kalyan's proposition is range and visibility — thousands of designs on display, with the day's gold rate and making charges presented as a matter of routine.

VisitBest recommendation: Look at Kalyan for wedding shopping where you want to compare many regional bridal styles under one roof, in India or the Gulf.

3. Malabar Gold & Diamonds

Headquarters: Kozhikode, Kerala  |  Founded: 1993  |  Focus: Gold and diamond jewellery with a large Gulf and international network

Quick highlights:

  • Founded in 1993 in Kozhikode by M. P. Ahammed, who had earlier traded in spices and copra, with a first small shop in his home town
  • Markets a written set of customer assurances, the Malabar Promise, covering matters such as transparent pricing, buy-back and exchange terms
  • One of the most internationally spread Indian jewellers, with showrooms across the Gulf, South-East Asia and beyond alongside its Indian network

Malabar began, in chairman M. P. Ahammed's telling, with a conviction that customers stay loyal to whoever sells them pure gold at a fair, openly worked-out price — even if the margin is thinner. From Kozhikode in 1993 the group grew first through Kerala and then, from 2008, across the Gulf, following the Malayali diaspora; it now runs showrooms in many countries and is counted among the world's larger jewellery retailers in industry rankings such as Deloitte's Global Powers of Luxury Goods. Its stores sell gold, diamond, platinum and gemstone jewellery with named collections for bridal, festive and daily wear. The group's structure is unusual: thousands of small investors, including employees, hold stakes in the business, a model the company itself highlights as the basis of its transparency.

VisitBest recommendation: Consider Malabar if you split your life between India and the Gulf — the same brand, policies and service network follow you in both places.

4. Joyalukkas

Headquarters: Thrissur, Kerala  |  Founded: 1987 (family roots to 1956)  |  Focus: Large showrooms, gold and diamond jewellery across India and the Gulf

Quick highlights:

  • The group's roots are a small Thrissur store opened in 1956 by Alukkas Varghese; his son Joy Alukkas opened the first overseas store in Abu Dhabi in 1987 and built the Joyalukkas brand from it
  • Entered Indian retail at the start of the 2000s and expanded through Kerala and the rest of India, alongside a large Gulf presence
  • Known for very large format stores, including one of the world's biggest jewellery showrooms in Chennai, as the group itself notes

Joyalukkas is the Gulf-first branch of Thrissur's Alukkas jewellery family. Joy Alukkas took the family's trade to Abu Dhabi in 1987, survived the Gulf War disruption, and built a chain across the Emirates before bringing the format home to Kerala in the early 2000s. The stores are deliberately grand — wide floors of gold, diamond and precious-stone jewellery aimed squarely at the wedding and festival buyer — and the brand leans on the trust vocabulary of the Kerala gold market, where it competes with Kalyan, Malabar and Jos Alukkas within a few streets of its home town. Beyond jewellery, the group runs money-exchange, mall and real-estate businesses, but jewellery remains the flagship.

VisitBest recommendation: Look at Joyalukkas for big-occasion gold shopping, particularly in Kerala and the Gulf, where its largest showrooms are.

5. Tribhovandas Bhimji Zaveri (TBZ — The Original)

Headquarters: Zaveri Bazaar, Mumbai, Maharashtra  |  Founded: 1864  |  Focus: Wedding and occasion jewellery, strongest in Maharashtra and Gujarat

Quick highlights:

  • Founded in 1864 in Mumbai's Zaveri Bazaar and run by five generations of the Zaveri family — the oldest name in this list by a wide margin
  • The company says it introduced a jewellery buy-back guarantee as early as 1938 and was among the first in India to sell fully hallmarked jewellery
  • In 2026, Chennai-based GRT Jewellers agreed to acquire a controlling stake in TBZ from the promoter family, according to The Hindu BusinessLine — a landmark change for the 162-year-old house

TBZ predates the Indian republic, the railways' golden age and the very idea of branded retail. It began in 1864 as a single store in Zaveri Bazaar, the dense Mumbai lane that remains the heart of India's gold trade, and grew on one asset: a name that Maharashtrian and Gujarati families trusted for wedding gold across generations. The company professionalised early — a public listing in 2012, stores across western and central India — while staying family-led through five generations. That era is now closing: in 2026 GRT Jewellers agreed to buy the promoters' controlling stake, a deal the business press covered as the end of one of Indian retail's longest family runs. The stores, the name and the wedding focus continue; the ownership story is the thing to watch.

VisitBest recommendation: Choose TBZ for a heritage wedding purchase in Maharashtra or Gujarat — and, while the ownership transition completes, confirm current store policies at the showroom as you would anywhere.

6. Senco Gold & Diamonds

Headquarters: Kolkata, West Bengal  |  Founded: 1938  |  Focus: Handcrafted Bengali gold work, bridal and lightweight jewellery

Quick highlights:

  • Traces its origin to 1938 in Kolkata, where the Sen family established the business; the modern company was incorporated in 1994 and listed in 2023
  • Built on Bengal's karigar tradition — the intricate, lightweight handcrafted gold work Kolkata's goldsmiths are known for
  • Runs Everlite, a sub-brand of lightweight gold and diamond jewellery aimed at everyday wear, alongside its main bridal-led stores

Senco is eastern India's jewellery house. Founded in Kolkata in 1938, it grew within a city whose goldsmiths — many of them Bengali karigars who supply jewellers across India — are famous for filigree-fine, handcrafted work that looks substantial without being heavy. That craftsmanship is Senco's signature: traditional Bengali bridal pieces, antique-finish and temple-inspired designs, and modern lightweight lines sit in the same store. The company is still led by the Sen family, professionalised over the last decade and took the business public in 2023. Its strongest footprint remains West Bengal and the east, with stores spreading across the country. For buyers who find South Indian bridal gold heavy and North Indian sets too plain, Senco's Bengali middle path is exactly the appeal.

VisitBest recommendation: Go to Senco for handcrafted, lightweight Bengali-style gold — especially bridal pieces that carry detail without excessive weight.

7. GRT Jewellers

Headquarters: Chennai, Tamil Nadu  |  Founded: 1964  |  Focus: South Indian bridal and temple jewellery

Quick highlights:

  • Founded in 1964 in Chennai by G. Rajendran as G.R. Thanga Maligai, and still run by the founder's family
  • A byword in Tamil Nadu for traditional bridal gold, including temple jewellery, and for silver articles, where it is a major retailer
  • In 2026 it agreed to acquire a controlling stake in Mumbai's TBZ, its biggest step towards becoming a national chain

Ask a Chennai family where wedding gold comes from and GRT is the likely answer. G. Rajendran opened the first store in 1964 in what became the T. Nagar shopping district, and the business — G.R. Thanga Maligai, literally a palace of gold — grew with the city's bridal market: heavy, traditional Tamil sets, temple jewellery modelled on Chola-era motifs, and a silver business large enough to be a destination in itself. The second generation has expanded GRT across the southern states and to Singapore while keeping the formula intact. Its 2026 agreement to take control of TBZ gives this Chennai house a western-India heritage brand overnight, and makes GRT one of the most interesting companies in the trade to watch.

VisitBest recommendation: Choose GRT for authentic Tamil bridal and temple jewellery, and for silver — few retailers stock either at this depth.

8. Jos Alukkas

Headquarters: Thrissur, Kerala  |  Founded: 1964  |  Focus: Large-format 'gold supermarket' stores, BIS 916 hallmarked gold

Quick highlights:

  • Founded in 1964 in Thrissur by Alukka Varghese and built up by his son Jos Alukka, whose sons now help run the group
  • Credited with pioneering the 'gold supermarket' — very large self-browsing jewellery stores — in Kerala, a format rivals later adopted
  • Its own site emphasises BIS 916 hallmarked 22-karat gold across its showrooms, a purity standardisation push the brand has long championed

Jos Alukkas is the third great Thrissur name in this list, and its story runs parallel to Joyalukkas: both descend from the same Alukkas family trade begun in the mid-twentieth century, and the businesses were formally separated in 2001. Jos Alukka's contribution to the format was scale — the 'gold supermarket', a large store where a family could browse thousands of pieces at leisure rather than across a small counter. The chain remains concentrated in the southern states, sells gold, diamond and platinum jewellery, and was an early mover online among Kerala jewellers, with its own e-commerce store and digital gold products. Purity messaging — BIS 916 hallmarking on its 22-karat gold — is central to how the brand presents itself.

VisitBest recommendation: Consider Jos Alukkas in the southern states for large-format stores and a straightforward, hallmark-led approach to 22-karat gold.

9. Bhima Jewellers

Headquarters: Kerala (founded in Alappuzha)  |  Founded: 1925  |  Focus: Ready-made gold jewellery, Kerala and South Indian bridal

Quick highlights:

  • Founded in 1925 in Alappuzha (Alleppey) by K. Bhima Bhattar and still family-run, now by the founder's sons under one brand
  • Credited with pioneering ready-made jewellery retail in Kerala — finished ornaments sold off the counter at a time when most gold was made to order
  • Showrooms across Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, with a presence in the UAE; its Thiruvananthapuram flagship has drawn record-setting single-day sales, as reported in 2024

Bhima turned a hundred years old in 2025, and its founding idea sounds obvious only in hindsight: sell finished jewellery, ready to wear, instead of asking every customer to commission a piece and wait. K. Bhima Bhattar opened in Alappuzha in 1925, built the business on purity assurances, and his sons later divided territories while keeping one brand — a structure the group has since unified under a single marketing umbrella. Bhima's heartland is Kerala, where its showrooms are wedding-season landmarks, with stores across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka and in the Emirates. A Kerala institution rather than a national advertiser, it rewards the buyer who shops where the locals do.

VisitBest recommendation: Look at Bhima in Kerala for traditional bridal gold from a century-old house — its unified brand now covers the family's stores across the south.

10. PC Jeweller

Headquarters: New Delhi  |  Founded: 2005  |  Focus: Hallmarked gold and certified diamond jewellery, large-format stores

Quick highlights:

  • A first-generation business founded in 2005 by brothers Padam Chand Gupta and Balram Garg, opening its first showroom in Delhi's Karol Bagh market
  • Positioned itself from the start on selling only hallmarked gold and certified diamond jewellery, before hallmarking became mandatory
  • Went through a difficult period of high debt and store closures after 2018 and has since been restructuring and reducing borrowings, as widely reported in the business press

PC Jeweller is the youngest of the big northern names and the one with the most dramatic arc. Founded in 2005 in Karol Bagh — Delhi's wholesale jewellery district — it expanded fast through the early 2010s on a simple pitch: large-format stores, hallmarked gold and certified diamonds, in a market still dominated by small family shops. It listed, grew to dozens of showrooms, and then hit a severe debt and governance crisis from 2018 that shrank the network and the business. Recent years have been about repair: closing weak stores, cutting debt and refocusing on stronger locations. The brand remains a significant northern retailer, and its showrooms still trade on the original hallmarked-and-certified proposition — but it is a chain rebuilding, not one at its peak.

VisitBest recommendation: Consider PC Jeweller in the north for certified diamond jewellery at large-format stores — and read the buy-back and exchange terms at the counter, as you should with any jeweller.

11. Khazana Jewellery

Headquarters: Chennai, Tamil Nadu  |  Founded: 1989  |  Focus: South Indian gold and bridal jewellery, in-house crafted designs

Quick highlights:

  • Founded by Kishore Kumar Jain, who opened the first showroom on NSC Bose Road, Chennai in 1989; the Cathedral Road flagship followed in 1993
  • Built around in-house manufacturing with its own karigars, at a time when most retailers outsourced production
  • Concentrated in the southern states, with its deepest presence in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana

Khazana — the name means 'treasure' — is Chennai's home-grown challenger to the Kerala and national chains. Kishore Kumar Jain came from a family gold business and set up in Chennai in 1989, betting on control of production: Khazana made its own jewellery with employed craftsmen when outsourcing was the trade's norm, which let it push distinctive, design-led stock rather than the market's standard patterns. The Cathedral Road showroom, opened in 1993, made its name, and the chain spread through the southern states. It remains privately held and family-led, with a loyal Tamil and Telugu customer base that treats it as a first-choice wedding jeweller.

VisitBest recommendation: Look at Khazana in Chennai and the south for design-led bridal gold from a retailer that manufactures much of what it sells.

12. Waman Hari Pethe Jewellers (WHP)

Headquarters: Mumbai (Girgaon), Maharashtra  |  Founded: 1909  |  Focus: Maharashtrian traditional jewellery and wedding gold

Quick highlights:

  • Founded in 1909 in Girgaon, Mumbai by brothers Waman Hari Pethe and Ganesh Hari Pethe, and still run by the Pethe family, now in its fifth generation
  • Began in pearl and gold trading and built its name on purity testing practices it introduced itself, decades before formal hallmarking existed
  • The definitive name for Maharashtrian bridal jewellery — mangalsutra, thushi, mohanmala and Kolhapuri styles — with stores across Maharashtra and in Goa and Indore, per the trade press

If TBZ is Zaveri Bazaar's grand old house, WHP is Maharashtra's family jeweller. The Pethe brothers started in Girgaon in 1909 dealing in pearls and gold, and the business grew with middle-class Mumbai — Dadar, Thane, Borivali and Pune rather than the wholesale lanes. Its specialisation is the Maharashtrian bridal trousseau: the thushi choker, the mohanmala, Kolhapuri saaj and the black-bead mangalsutra in its many regional forms, stocked in a depth the national chains rarely attempt. The family has also modernised — diamond and contemporary lines, online selling, and stores beyond Maharashtra — but the brand's centre of gravity remains the Marathi wedding, which it has dressed for five generations.

VisitBest recommendation: Choose WHP for Maharashtrian wedding jewellery in Mumbai and Pune — the regional range here is the point of the store.

13. Reliance Jewels

Headquarters: Mumbai, Maharashtra (Reliance Retail)  |  Founded: 2007  |  Focus: National chain retailing regional Indian design traditions

Quick highlights:

  • The jewellery format of Reliance Retail, launched in 2007 with a first showroom in Bengaluru — the second corporate entry into a trade then dominated by family firms, after the Tata group's Tanishq
  • Stocks regional specialities from across India — Amritsari jadau, Jaipur kundan, Kolkata filigree, Kerala temple work — under one roof, as its store descriptions detail
  • Runs both standalone showrooms and shop-in-shop counters inside other Reliance formats

Reliance Jewels is what happens when India's largest retailer decides jewellery deserves a format. Reliance Retail launched it in 2007, a decade after Tanishq had proven a corporation could sell gold, and rolled it out with the group's characteristic speed. The pitch differs from the heritage houses: no founding family, no single regional tradition, but a pan-Indian catalogue — jadau from Amritsar, kundan from Jaipur, filigree from Kolkata, temple jewellery from Kerala — sold with corporate systems behind it, including in-store purity testing and standardised policies. Stores sit in high streets and inside Reliance's other retail formats. For a buyer in a city without a strong regional chain, it is often the most available organised option.

VisitBest recommendation: Consider Reliance Jewels for a corporate, policy-standardised purchase — especially in cities where the big regional chains are absent.

How to Buy Gold Jewellery in India: Hallmarks, Making Charges and Buy-Back

Read the hallmark — all three parts of it. Since June 2021, BIS hallmarking has been mandatory for gold jewellery sold in India, rolled out in phases across districts and now covering most of the country. A genuine hallmark has three elements stamped on the piece: the BIS logo; the purity and fineness mark — 22K916 means 22-karat gold of 916 parts per thousand fine gold (18K750 and 14K585 work the same way); and the HUID, a six-character alphanumeric code unique to that individual piece.

Verify the HUID yourself. Download the BIS Care app, use its 'Verify HUID' function and type the code from the piece in front of you. The app returns the jeweller and the item details recorded at hallmarking. If the code on the jewellery does not resolve, or the description does not match the piece, do not complete the purchase. This two-minute check is the single most valuable habit in modern gold buying — it works at a national chain and at a single-store jeweller alike.

Understand the bill before you admire the piece. Your payable amount is built from the gold value (the day's rate for that purity, multiplied by the net gold weight), plus stone charges where applicable, plus making charges, plus GST — charged at 3% on jewellery and shown on the bill. Insist on an itemised bill that states purity, gross and net weight, stone weight and value separately, and the making charge as its own line. A bill that shows only a lump sum is a bill designed to be unchallengeable later.

Making charges are negotiable and vary for real reasons. They are billed either per gram or as a percentage of the gold value, and they pay for the work in the piece — a machine-made chain and a hand-filgreed Bengali bridal set honestly cost different amounts of labour. What you should not accept is vagueness: ask the rate, ask whether it is per gram or percentage, and compare the same design's total at two stores on the same day. Older bills sometimes showed a separate 'wastage' head for gold lost in making; most organised retailers now fold that into the making charge, so if wastage appears as its own line, ask what it covers.

Buy-back and exchange are policies, not rights. Every retailer sets its own terms: typically the gold is credited at the current rate for its purity while making charges are not refunded, and stone values may be credited at a discount or not at all. The differences between two jewellers' buy-back terms can be worth more over a lifetime of exchanges than a small difference in making charges today. Get the current policy in writing — on the bill or the store's printed terms — before you pay, at every store in this list and every store outside it.

For diamonds, the certificate is the product. A certified stone should come with a certificate from an established laboratory naming its carat, cut, colour and clarity, and the details on the certificate should match the stone you are buying. Ask which lab certifies the retailer's diamonds and whether uncertified smaller stones are set in the same piece — a normal practice, but one that should be stated, not discovered.

Also Worth Knowing

Monthly gold schemes need a careful read. Most chains in this list run advance-purchase schemes — pay monthly instalments, buy jewellery at the end, often with the jeweller adding a bonus instalment.
