They suit disciplined wedding saving, but they are retailer-run arrangements, not bank deposits: read what happens if you stop paying, whether the bonus survives an early exit, and whether the gold rate is fixed at payment or at purchase.

Old-gold exchange is priced by testing, not sentiment. When you exchange old jewellery, the store will test its purity — by X-ray fluorescence or, for an exact figure, by melting — and credit you for the fine gold actually present. Jewellery bought before hallmarking may test below its stamped claim, and stones and enamel are excluded from the weight. A transparent store does the testing in front of you and shows the reading; that showroom behaviour is itself a useful way to judge any jeweller in this guide.

FAQs

Which is the oldest jeweller in this list?

Tribhovandas Bhimji Zaveri (TBZ), founded in 1864 in Mumbai's Zaveri Bazaar — older than the next name here, Waman Hari Pethe (1909), by 45 years. India also has individual family firms with very long histories; TBZ is the oldest of the scaled retail chains profiled in this guide.

What does 22K916 on a hallmark mean?

It is two ways of saying the same thing: 22-karat gold, which is 916 parts fine gold per thousand (91.6%). The other common marks are 18K750 and 14K585. The fineness number is what determines the gold's value per gram, so it is the part of the hallmark to check against your bill.

What is the HUID, and how do I check it?

The HUID is a six-character unique identification number assigned to each hallmarked piece when it is assayed. Enter it under 'Verify HUID' in the BIS Care app to see the recorded jeweller and item details. A piece whose HUID does not verify should not be bought.

Why do making charges differ so much between jewellers?

Because they pay for different things: hand labour versus machine production, design complexity, and each retailer's pricing strategy — some chains compete on low making charges for simple pieces and price intricate bridal work higher. Compare total bills for comparable designs on the same day rather than headline percentages, and remember that making charges are generally not returned on buy-back.

Which jeweller is best for wedding jewellery?

The one whose design tradition matches the wedding. Tamil bridal and temple sets point to GRT or Khazana; Bengali handcrafted work to Senco; Maharashtrian trousseau pieces to WHP or TBZ; Kerala bridal gold to Bhima, Jos Alukkas, Kalyan or Malabar; and a national, standardised purchase to Tanishq. Wedding jewellery is regional clothing in gold — buy it from the house that speaks that language.

How were these 13 jewellers selected?

Editorially, by VisitBest: national scale, regional dominance, historical significance, or a distinctive proposition a buyer should know about — the same test applied across our company guides. It is not a ranking, and inclusion is not an endorsement of any store's current prices or policies, which you should confirm at the counter.

Conclusion

India's jewellery trade is a ladder from the family store to the listed chain, and this guide profiles the 13 names that define its top rungs — the 1864 house in Zaveri Bazaar, the Kerala giants, the regional masters of Tamil, Bengali and Maharashtrian gold, and the corporate formats of Titan and Reliance. Choose by the design tradition you are buying, the region you are buying in, and the paperwork you are offered. Check the HUID, itemise the bill, and take the buy-back terms in writing, and any jeweller on this list — or off it — will serve you well.

Research note: Company facts — headquarters, founding years and focus — are taken from the companies' own websites and reputable public sources, including company profiles and reporting by The Hindu BusinessLine, Forbes India, Business Standard and the Financial Express; the full source list is held with this article's research file. Store counts, revenues and market rankings change constantly and are deliberately not stated as league tables. Logos are the companies' own, taken from their official websites; TBZ — The Original is profiled without one because its website would not release the file to us, and no substitute image has been used.

excerpt.rendered: Profile the 13 leading jewellers in India — Tanishq, Kalyan Jewellers, Malabar Gold & Diamonds, TBZ, Senco, GRT and more — each with its headquarters, founding year and what it is known for, in an editorial selection that explains how the market is organised instead of pretending to rank it, plus a plain-language guide to BIS hallmarking, HUID checks, making charges and buy-back terms.

title.rendered: Famous Punjabi Singers: 15 Legendary Voices From Folk Roots to Global Charts

content.rendered:
The most famous Punjabi singers include Surinder Kaur, Gurdas Maan, Amar Singh Chamkila, Kuldeep Manak, Hans Raj Hans, Daler Mehndi, Diljit Dosanjh, Sidhu Moose Wala, AP Dhillon and Karan Aujla. Together they trace the full arc of Punjabi music — from the folk songs sung at village fairs and on All India Radio, through the cassette and bhangra-pop booms, to the streaming era in which Punjabi artists headline Coachella, top Billboard charts and sell out arenas on four continents.

This is an editorial selection by the VisitBest team, not an official ranking. Punjabi music has produced hundreds of beloved voices across a century of recording, and any list of fifteen will leave out favourites; the singers below were chosen because each one changed the sound, the audience or the business of Punjabi music in a way that can be documented, not just felt.

Every fact here — birth and death dates, signature songs, awards and chart records — was checked against published reference sources and reputable reporting, and each singer's sources are listed on this page. Thirteen of the fifteen singers are shown in photographs verified on Wikimedia Commons. Amar Singh Chamkila and Kuldeep Manak are profiled in words alone, because no verifiably correct, freely licensed photograph of either artist could be confirmed; rather than publish a picture of the wrong person — a common error with older Punjabi artists — we have left their sections without an image and said so plainly.

Quick Answer — Famous Punjabi Singers at a Glance

If you only have a minute, start here. Punjabi music's defining voices fall into three broad generations: the folk legends who preserved the tradition on radio and record; the bhangra-pop stars who took the sound worldwide in the 1990s; and the streaming-era artists, many of them based in Canada, who now compete on global charts. The full profiles follow below.

  1. Surinder Kaur — the "Nightingale of Punjab" who carried Punjabi folk song to national audiences.
  2. Amar Singh Chamkila — the "Elvis of Punjab", the best-selling Punjabi artist of the cassette era.
  3. Kuldeep Manak — the "Kaliyan da Badshah", king of the Punjabi narrative ballad.
  4. Gurdas Maan — the living legend, and the only Punjabi singer to win a National Film Award for playback singing.
  5. Hans Raj Hans — the Sufi-folk master and Padma Shri recipient.
  6. Daler Mehndi — the man who made bhangra a global pop phenomenon.
  7. Sukhbir — the "Prince of Bhangra" who fused bhangra with rap, reggae and techno.
  8. Babbu Maan — the singer-songwriter whose own words built a fiercely loyal audience.
  9. Diljit Dosanjh — the first Indian Punjabi artist to perform at Coachella.
  10. Sidhu Moose Wala — the Brampton-raised star who fused Punjabi folk with hip-hop and broke streaming records.
  11. Ammy Virk — the folk-rooted singer who became one of Punjabi cinema's biggest actors.
  12. Jasmine Sandlas — the California-raised singer-songwriter who broke through in Bollywood.
  13. AP Dhillon — the first Punjabi-language artist to perform at Canada's Juno Awards.
  14. Karan Aujla — the "Geetan Di Machine", songwriter turned chart-topping solo star.
  15. Shubh — the streaming-first phenomenon who rose without a single film song.

How Punjabi Music Travelled From Village Fairs to Global Charts

Punjabi music begins with folk forms built for open-air performance: the long narrative ballads called kali and qissa, wedding songs, and devotional Sufi poetry, accompanied by instruments such as the tumbi, algoza and dhol. Recorded music changed everything. From the 1940s, singers like Surinder Kaur took those village forms into radio studios and onto shellac records, fixing a repertoire of folk standards that is still sung today.

The 1980s cassette boom created the first Punjabi superstar economy. Cheap cassettes and powerful live akhara performances made Amar Singh Chamkila the best-selling artist of his era, while Kuldeep Manak preserved the oldest storytelling forms on record. In the 1990s, satellite television and a wealthy diaspora in Britain, Canada and the United States turned bhangra into pop: Daler Mehndi's and Sukhbir's albums sold in the millions and played at weddings on every continent.

The streaming era completed the journey. YouTube and Spotify let Canada-based artists such as Sidhu Moose Wala, AP Dhillon, Karan Aujla and Shubh build global audiences without radio or film support, while Diljit Dosanjh carried Punjabi music onto the Coachella stage and the Billboard charts. The fifteen singers below are the essential names in that story.

The Legends Who Built Punjabi Music

1. Surinder Kaur

Punjabi folk · Active 1943–2006 · "Nightingale of Punjab"

Quick highlights:

  • Known as the "Nightingale of Punjab" (Punjab di Koyal)
  • Made her first live performance on Lahore Radio in August 1943
  • Recorded more than 2,000 songs, as widely reported
  • Received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1984) and the Padma Shri (2006)

Surinder Kaur (25 November 1929 – 14 June 2006) is credited with pioneering and popularising Punjabi folk song. Singing on Lahore Radio as a teenager in 1943, she was among the first voices to carry the repertoire of Punjabi village folk — wedding songs, laments and love lyrics — to a mass audience, and her recordings of songs such as "Maavan te Dheeyan", "Jutti Kasuri", "Madhaniyan", "Lathe Di Chadar", "Kaala Doria" and "Bajre Da Sitta" remain the reference versions. Between 1948 and 1952 she also sang playback for Hindi films, beginning with Shaheed (1948), before Punjabi folk music became her life's work.

Why she matters: almost every later singer on this list learned the folk repertoire through her recordings. She turned a regional folk tradition into a recorded canon, and the state honoured her for it with the Padma Shri in 2006, months before her death in New Jersey on 14 June 2006.

2. Amar Singh Chamkila

Folk duets and social commentary · Active 1979–1988 · "Elvis of Punjab"

Quick highlights:

  • Widely called the "Elvis of Punjab"
  • Recorded his first song, the duet "Takue Te Takua", in 1980
  • Reported to be the highest-selling Punjabi artist of his era
  • His life was dramatised in Imtiaz Ali's 2024 Netflix film Amar Singh Chamkila

Amar Singh Chamkila (born Dhani Ram, 21 July 1960 – 8 March 1988) came from Dugri, near Ludhiana, and rose with astonishing speed after his first recorded duet, "Takue Te Takua" (1980), sung with Surinder Sonia. Performing with his wife and singing partner Amarjot, he dominated Punjab's live akhara circuit and cassette market through the 1980s with songs such as "Pehle Lalkare Naal", the devotional "Baba Tera Nankana" and "Talwar Main Kalgidhar Di". His lyrics — earthy, funny and sharply observant about village life — made him both hugely popular and controversial. On 8 March 1988, Chamkila, Amarjot and two members of their band were shot dead in Mehsampur village; the killings remain unsolved. He was 27 years old.

Why he matters: Chamkila proved a Punjabi folk singer could outsell everyone through cassettes and live shows alone. Nearly four decades later his songs are still covered constantly, and the 2024 biographical film — in which Diljit Dosanjh, himself on this list, played Chamkila — introduced him to a new global generation.

3. Kuldeep Manak

Kali folk ballads · Active 1968–2011 · "Kaliyan da Badshah"

Quick highlights:

  • Known as the "Kaliyan da Badshah" — King of Kaliyan
  • Master of the kali, the long Punjabi narrative ballad
  • His signature kali was "Tere Tille Ton", the story of Heer
  • A statue of Manak stands in Ludhiana

Kuldeep Manak (born Latif Mohammed Khan, 15 November 1951 – 30 November 2011) was the supreme exponent of the kali — the demanding, long-form narrative ballad at the heart of Punjabi folk tradition. Beginning his career in 1968 with duets alongside Harcharan Grewal and Seema, he devoted himself to singing the great Punjabi qisse: the romances and legends of Heer, Mirza-Sahiban and Dulla Bhatti, holding audiences for the length of an epic in a single performance. His most famous recording, the kali "Tere Tille Ton" (which opens by describing Heer's beauty), is regarded as the benchmark of the form.

Why he matters: where others shortened folk songs for radio, Manak preserved Punjab's storytelling tradition at full length and at the highest standard. Folk singers still measure themselves against his kalis, and his death on 30 November 2011 closed the classical era of the form.

4. Gurdas Maan

Folk and film · Active 1980–present · National Film Award winner

Quick highlights:

  • Shot to national fame with "Dil Da Mamla Hai" on Doordarshan in 1980
  • The only Punjabi singer to win the National Film Award for Best Male Playback Singer
  • Has released more than 34 albums and written over 305 songs
  • Received the Filmfare Award for Living Legend in 2017

Gurdas Maan (born 4 January 1957, Giddarbaha) is Punjabi music's most decorated living figure. After "Dil Da Mamla Hai" (1980) made him a national name, songs such as "Chhalla" — from the film Long Da Lishkara (1983), composed by Jagjit Singh — established him as both a folk singer and a film star. For the film Waris Shah: Ishq Daa Waaris he sang the entire story of Heer in the traditional style, winning the National Film Award for Best Male Playback Singer at the 54th National Film Awards — an honour no other Punjabi singer has received. His album Boot Polishan won Best International Album at the UK Asian Music Awards in 2009, and in 2015 he performed "Ki Banu Duniya Da" with Diljit Dosanjh on Coke Studio, a symbolic meeting of generations.

Why he matters: Maan kept the folk and Sufi core of Punjabi music intact while taking it to national film honours and international awards. For more than four decades he has been the standard against which Punjabi singer-actors are judged.

5. Hans Raj Hans

Folk and Sufi · Active 1983–present · Padma Shri 2008

Quick highlights:

  • Trained by the renowned teacher Ustad Puran Shah Koti
  • Received the Padma Shri in 2008
  • Sang with Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan for the film Kachche Dhaage (1999)
  • His "Dil Chori Sada Ho Gaya" was remade for Sonu Ke Titu Ki Sweety (2018)

Hans Raj Hans (born 9 April 1962, Shafipur, near Jalandhar) built his art on classical discipline: trained by Ustad Puran Shah Koti, he became a master of Punjabi folk and Sufi singing, releasing albums from Jogian De Kanna Vich (1983) onwards and carrying the Sufi repertoire to concert stages worldwide. His voice crossed into Hindi cinema with songs for Kachche Dhaage (1999) — where he sang alongside Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan — Monsoon Wedding (2001), Nayak (2001) and "Ik Tu Hi Tu Hi" in Mausam (2011). India honoured him with the Padma Shri in 2008. He later served as a Member of Parliament for North West Delhi from 2019 to 2024.

Why he matters: Hans Raj Hans is the bridge between the mehfil tradition of Sufi singing and the mainstream — a folk singer with a classical guru's training whose voice defined the devotional soul of modern Punjabi music.

The Pop Era — Bhangra Goes Global

6. Daler Mehndi

Bhangra pop · Active 1995–present · The voice of "Tunak Tunak Tun"

Quick highlights:

  • Debut album Bolo Ta Ra Ra (1995) was reported to have sold over 20 million copies
  • Credited with making bhangra popular worldwide and Indi-pop independent of film music
  • "Tunak Tunak Tun" (1998) became a global internet-era hit
  • Founded his own label, D Records, in 2000

Daler Mehndi (born Daler Singh, 18 August 1967, Patna) took bhangra out of Punjab and made it pop. His debut album Bolo Ta Ra Ra (1995) was reported to have sold more than 20 million copies, and its follow-up Dardi Rab Rab (1996) sold even more, establishing Indi-pop as a commercial force separate from Bollywood. In 1998 he released "Tunak Tunak Tun", whose video — made on a then-unprecedented budget of about ₹2.5 crore — put him dancing against chroma-key landscapes; years later the song became a worldwide internet phenomenon, and its dance was even used as a character animation in the game World of Warcraft.

Why he matters: Mehndi created the template of the Punjabi pop superstar: the jewel-toned turbans, the arena energy, the album as an event. Every Punjabi pop act since has worked in the space he opened.

7. Sukhbir

Bhangra pop · Active 1996–present · "Prince of Bhangra"

Quick highlights:

  • Known as the "Prince of Bhangra"
  • His debut album New Stylee won three Channel V Awards in 1996
  • "Ishq Tera Tadpave (Oh Ho Ho Ho)" (1999) remains a wedding staple
  • The Hindu described him as a "pioneer in bhangra pop"

Sukhbir Singh (born 9 November 1969, Bhogpur, Jalandhar district) was raised largely in Nairobi, Kenya, and has been based in Dubai since 1992 — a biography that explains his sound. His debut album New Stylee, recorded in Dubai, won Best Debut Album, Best Male Vocalist and Best Music Video ("Punjabi Munde") at the 1996 Channel V Awards. Gal Ban Gayi went platinum in 1997, and "Ishq Tera Tadpave" (1999) became one of the most durable party songs in Indian music; it found a second life in the film Hindi Medium (2017), and he returned to Bollywood with "Sauda Khara Khara" in Good Newwz (2019). His later single "Nachdi" (2021) reached number 4 on Billboard's Top Triller Global chart.

Why he matters: Sukhbir fused bhangra with rap, techno and reggae years before "fusion" became a marketing word, proving Punjabi pop could be engineered for dancefloors from Dubai to Toronto.

8. Babbu Maan

Singer-songwriter folk-pop · Active 1997–present

Quick highlights:

  • Writes, composes and sings his own songs
  • Breakthrough album Saaun Di Jhadi (2001) made him a star in Punjab
  • His album Talaash: In Search of Soul (2013) entered Billboard's World Albums top 10
  • Won four World Music Awards in 2014, including World's Best Indian Male Artist

Babbu Maan (born Tejinder Singh Maan, 29 March 1975, Khant Maanpur, Fatehgarh Sahib district) is the auteur of this list: a singer-songwriter who writes his own lyrics and built his audience on the strength of his words. After early albums Sajjan Rumaal De Geya (1997) and Tu Meri Miss India (1999), the album Saaun Di Jhadi (2001) — with "Chan Chandni", "Dil Ta Pagal Hai" and "Kabza" — made him a phenomena in Punjab, and Pyaas (2005) became one of the best-selling Punjabi albums of its time. He was named Best International Artist at the Brit Asia TV Music Awards in 2010, and he has also written, produced and starred in films including Hashar (2008) and Ekam (2010).

Why he matters: Babbu Maan showed that a Punjabi singer could build a decades-long, fiercely loyal following on songwriting alone — his concerts in Punjab still draw some of the largest crowds in the industry.

The Streaming Generation

9. Diljit Dosanjh

Pop and film · Active 2003–present · Coachella and Billboard record-maker

Quick highlights:

  • First Indian Punjabi artist to perform at Coachella (April 2023)
  • His album G.O.A.T. (2020) put him on Billboard's Social 50 chart
  • Won the Filmfare Award for Best Male Debut for Udta Punjab (2016)
  • Played Amar Singh Chamkila in the 2024 film Amar Singh Chamkila, earning an International Emmy nomination

Diljit Dosanjh (born 6 January 1984, Dosanjh Kalan, Jalandhar district) began with the album Ishq Da Uda Ada (2003) and built his following steadily through albums such as The Next Level (2009) and Back 2 Basics (2012); his single "Proper Patola" (2013) was the first Punjabi song featured on Vevo. In the 2020s he went fully global: G.O.A.T. (2020) topped Billboard's Top Triller Global chart, Moonchild Era (2021) reached number 32 on the Billboard Canadian Albums chart making him the first Indian artist with three albums on the Billboard charts, and in April 2023 he became the first Indian Punjabi artist to perform at Coachella. As an actor he starred in Punjab 1984 (2014) and Jatt & Juliet (2012), won a Filmfare debut award for Udta Punjab, and in 2019 became the first turbaned Sikh honoured with a Madame Tussauds wax figure; his Dil-Luminati world tour of 2024 set records for an Indian artist.

Why he matters: Diljit is the proof of concept for the global Punjabi superstar — a turbaned, Punjabi-speaking artist headlining the world's biggest festival stages and film industries without diluting either.

10. Sidhu Moose Wala

Hip-hop and folk fusion · Active 2016–2022

Quick highlights:

  • His album Moosetape (2021) was the first Indian album to pass one billion streams on Spotify
  • First Indian singer to perform at London's Wireless Festival (2021)
  • Named by The Guardian among its 50 up-and-coming artists worldwide (2020)
  • Began as a songwriter; wrote the hit "License" for Ninja (2016)

Sidhu Moose Wala (born Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu, 11 June 1993, Moosa village, Mansa district) graduated in electrical engineering from Guru Nanak Dev Engineering College, Ludhiana, in 2016 and moved to Brampton, Canada, as a student. He broke through as a performer with "So High" (2017), made with producer Byg Byrd, which won him the Best Lyricist award at the Brit Asia TV Music Awards. His debut album PBX 1 (2018) charted in Canada, and Moosetape (2021) became a streaming landmark — its tracks charted on the Billboard Global 200 and Canadian Hot 100 while his collaboration "47" reached the UK Singles Chart top 20. Sidhu Moose Wala was shot dead on 29 May 2022, aged 28. We cover the case and its aftermath separately, in our explainer on the Sidhu Moose Wala murder case.

Why he matters: Moose Wala fused the cadences of Punjabi folk with hip-hop and wrote unflinchingly about village Punjab and the immigrant experience. In a six-year career he rewrote what a Punjabi artist's numbers could look like, and his music's audience has only grown since his death.

11. Ammy Virk

Folk-pop and film · Active 2011–present

Quick highlights:

  • His album Jattizm (2013) won Album of the Year at the PTC Punjabi Music Awards
  • Breakthrough song "Ikk Pal" spread virally while he was still a student
  • His films Angrej (2015) and Qismat (2018) are among the highest-grossing Punjabi films
  • Played cricketer Balwinder Sandhu in the Hindi film 83 (2021)

Ammy Virk (born Amninderpal Singh Virk, 11 May 1992, Lohar Majra, Nabha) was completing a biotechnology degree at Punjabi University, Patiala, when his song "Ikk Pal" went viral and turned him towards music full-time. His folk and Sufi-tinged singing, on songs such as "Qismat" (2017), "Haan Karde" and "Zindabad Yaarian", made him a fixture of Punjabi playlists, and his acting career ran in parallel: a prize-winning debut in Angrej (2015), the hit romance Qismat (2018), and Hindi films including Bhuj: The Pride of India (2021) and 83 (2021). He is recognised by his signature Patiala-Shahi turban.

Why he matters: Virk represents the folk-rooted singer-actor at his most bankable — proof that the oldest route into Punjabi music, a strong folk voice, still produces its biggest film stars.

12. Jasmine Sandlas

Pop, R&B and playback · Active 2007–present

Quick highlights:

  • Born in Punjab and raised in Stockton, California; writes her own songs
  • Bollywood breakthrough with "Yaar Na Miley" in Kick (2014)
  • "Illegal Weapon" and "Sip Sip" were remade for Street Dancer 3D (2020)
  • Won Most Popular Song of the Year at the PTC Punjabi Film Awards 2016 and a Screen Award for Best Female Playback

Jasmine Sandlas was born in Punjab and raised in Stockton, California, where West Coast hip-hop shaped her writing as much as Punjabi folk did. Her first song, "Muskan" (2007), was a hit, and her debut studio album Gulabi (2012) was produced by Bohemia. Her Bollywood playback debut, "Yaar Na Miley" for Kick (2014), went viral and topped charts; with Garry Sandhu and producer Intense she then delivered "Illegal Weapon" (2017) and "Sip Sip" (2018), both successful enough to be remade for the film Street Dancer 3D. Her later work includes the album What's in a Name (2020) and "Taras" for the film Munjya (2024).

Why she matters: Sandlas is one of the very few women to build a top-tier Punjabi singing career on her own songwriting, spanning the diaspora underground, PTC award stages and Bollywood playback.

13. AP Dhillon

Pop and R&B · Active 2019–present · Based in Canada

Quick highlights:

  • First Punjabi-language artist to perform at the Juno Awards (2023)
  • "Brown Munde" (2020) topped the UK Asian chart and entered Canada's Apple Music chart
  • All seven tracks of his EP Not by Chance (2020) charted in New Zealand
  • Subject of the 2023 Prime Video docuseries AP Dhillon: First of a Kind

AP Dhillon (born Amritpal Singh Dhillon, 10 January 1993, Mulianwali, Punjab) studied civil engineering before moving to Vancouver Island, Canada, and launching his own label, Run-Up Records, in 2019 with collaborators Gurinder Gill, Shinda Kahlon and producer Gminxr. His breakthrough year was 2020: "Majhail" topped the UK Asian and UK Punjabi charts, "Brown Munde" became a diaspora anthem that reached number one on the UK Asian chart, and "Excuses" topped the UK Punjabi chart. In 2023 he became the first Punjabi-language artist to perform at the Juno Awards, Canada's biggest music honours, and released the album The Brownprint in 2024.

Why he matters: Dhillon built a stadium-level career from a home studio in Canada, in Punjabi, without Bollywood or a major label — the clearest demonstration that the centre of Punjabi pop has moved to the diaspora.

14. Karan Aujla

Rap and pop · Active 2014–present · "Geetan Di Machine"

Quick highlights:

  • Known as "Geetan Di Machine" — the song machine — for his output as a writer
  • Began as a songwriter, writing "Range" for Jassi Gill and "G.O.A.T." for Diljit Dosanjh
  • His debut album Bacthafucup (2021) charted on the Billboard Canadian Albums chart
  • "Tauba Tauba" from Bad Newz (2024) topped the Billboard India chart; he won the Juno Fan Choice Award in 2024

Karan Aujla (born Jaskaran Singh Aujla, 18 January 1997, Ghurala, Ludhiana district) was writing hit songs for other singers while still at school — he gave Jassi Gill the lyrics of "Range" after meeting him at a wedding — and after moving to Canada in 2014 he wrote for artists including Jazzy B, Bohemia and Sukh-E while working part-time as a longshoreman in Surrey. As a performer he broke through with "Don't Worry" (2018), his first UK Asian chart entry; "Don't Look" spent more than 24 weeks on that chart. His albums Bacthafucup (2021) and Making Memories (2023), the latter debuting at number 5 on the Billboard Canadian Albums chart, established him as a solo star, and in 2024 his Bollywood song "Tauba Tauba" became one of the year's biggest Indian hits.

Why he matters: Aujla embodies the writer-first path of the new Punjabi industry: the pen that powered other stars' hits became, in the streaming era, a headline act in its own right.

15. Shubh

Hip-hop and trap · Active 2021–present · Based in Canada

Quick highlights:

  • Debut single "We Rollin" (2021) became a viral hit within months
  • "Baller" (2022), with producer Ikky, charted on the Canadian Hot 100
  • Debut album Still Rollin (2023) charted in Canada and New Zealand
  • Built his audience entirely through streaming, with no film songs

Shubh (born Shubhneet Singh, 10 August 1997, Nangal, Punjab) is based in Brampton, Ontario, and is the youngest artist on this list — and the purest product of the streaming age. He released his first single, "We Rollin", in September 2021, and it spread so fast that within a year his follow-ups "No Love" and "Baller" were charting internationally, "Baller" entering the Canadian Hot 100. His debut album Still Rollin (2023) charted on the Canadian Albums Chart and in New Zealand, with "Cheques" reaching number 3 on the Billboard India Songs chart. Shubh keeps a notably low public profile: the music, almost entirely written and performed by him, does the talking.

Why he matters: Shubh showed that a Punjabi artist can now go from a first upload to Billboard charts in under two years, with no label machine, no film placement and almost no interviews — a route that did not exist for any earlier generation on this list.

How These Singers Changed Punjabi Music

Read together, the fifteen careers above describe five shifts that define modern Punjabi music. First, preservation: Surinder Kaur and Kuldeep Manak recorded the folk repertoire — wedding songs, laments and epic ballads — before it could fade with the oral tradition. Second, the cassette economy: Chamkila's career proved that live performance and cheap tapes could make a folk singer the biggest commercial act in the state. Third, global pop: Daler Mehndi and Sukhbir engineered bhangra for satellite television and the diaspora wedding circuit, making Punjabi the party language of the Indian diaspora worldwide.

Fourth, the diaspora takeover: in the streaming era the industry's centre of gravity moved to Brampton, Surrey and Vancouver, where Moose Wala, AP Dhillon, Karan Aujla and Shubh built audiences bigger than Punjab itself could offer. And fifth, the mainstream breakthrough: Diljit Dosanjh at Coachella, Aujla's "Tauba Tauba" in a Bollywood blockbuster and Hans Raj Hans singing with Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan all mark moments when Punjabi music stopped being a regional category and became part of the global mainstream. Through every shift, the through-line is language pride — each generation found a new technology, from radio to Spotify, to keep Punjabi at the centre of the song.

Frequently Asked Questions About Famous Punjabi Singers

Who is the most famous Punjabi singer?
There is no single answer across eras. Gurdas Maan is the most decorated living legend; Diljit Dosanjh is currently the biggest global live draw, as the first Indian Punjabi artist to perform at Coachella; and Sidhu Moose Wala's streaming numbers made him the most-listened Punjabi artist of the streaming era. Historically, Surinder Kaur and Amar Singh Chamkila defined their generations.

Who is called the Nightingale of Punjab?
Surinder Kaur (1929–2006), also known in Punjabi as Punjab di Koyal. She is credited with pioneering and popularising Punjabi folk song and received the Padma Shri in 2006.

Who was known as the Elvis of Punjab?
Amar Singh Chamkila (1960–1988), the duet singer whose cassettes and live shows made him the highest-selling Punjabi artist of his era. He and his wife and singing partner Amarjot were killed in 1988; the case remains unsolved.

What is a kali in Punjabi music?
A kali is a long-form Punjabi narrative folk ballad, sung to tell stories such as Heer-Ranjha or Mirza-Sahiban in full. Kuldeep Manak, the "Kaliyan da Badshah" (King of Kaliyan), was its most celebrated exponent.

Which Punjabi singer performed at Coachella?
Diljit Dosanjh, in April 2023 — the first Indian Punjabi artist to perform at the festival. A year earlier, AP Dhillon had become the first Punjabi-language artist to perform at Canada's Juno Awards (2023).

Who is the Prince of Bhangra?
Sukhbir, the Dubai-based singer whose 1990s albums fused bhangra with rap, reggae and techno, and whose "Ishq Tera Tadpave (Oh Ho Ho Ho)" remains one of the most played Punjabi party songs ever recorded.

Conclusion — A Century of Punjabi Voices

From Surinder Kaur singing into a Lahore radio microphone in 1943 to Shubh topping charts from a home studio in Brampton, Punjabi music has repeatedly reinvented how it reaches its audience while refusing to change the language it sings in. These fifteen singers are not the whole story — no list could be — but they are its essential chapters: the folk canon, the cassette revolution, the bhangra-pop explosion and the streaming takeover, written by voices that each, in their own era, sounded like the future.

Research note: dates, songs, awards and chart facts were checked against the singers' reference biographies and reputable music reporting (sources include Encyclopaedia and reference entries, national broadsheets, Billboard and Official Charts reporting, and award records). title.rendered: Best Stainless Steel Pressure Cookers in India (2026)

content.rendered:
A pressure cooker is the hardest-working vessel in an Indian kitchen — dal, rice, khichdi, rajma and Sunday mutton all pass through it, often twice a day. More and more buyers are switching from aluminium to stainless steel for that daily workhorse: steel does not react with acidic food, does not pit or stain the way aluminium can, and has no coating to wear out. This guide compares the best stainless steel pressure cookers in India the practical way — ten real models from Hawkins, Prestige, Vinod, Pigeon by Stovekraft and Butterfly, each checked on Amazon.in, with its capacity, lid type, base construction and warranty spelt out so you can compare like with like.

Every model below was checked on Amazon.in in October 2026. We have deliberately not printed prices: cooker prices on Amazon.in move with sales, coupons and bank offers, sometimes within the same week. Use the Check price on Amazon buttons for the live price of the exact size you need before you buy.

Quick Answer

For one safe all-round buy, start with the Hawkins Contura Stainless Steel (SSC50) in 5 litres — a curved, inner-lid cooker with a thick sandwich bottom and a 5-year warranty — or the Prestige Deluxe Alpha Svachh if you prefer an outer lid, want its deep lid that controls frothing and spillage, and value the longest warranty here at 10 years. If even heating matters most, go tri-ply: the Hawkins Triply (HSST35) at 3.5 litres or the Vinod Platinum Triply at 5 litres. The Hawkins Futura Stainless Steel is the design icon, with fingertip pressure release instead of whistle-counting. On a tighter brief, the Butterfly Curve covers the basics with ISI certification and a 5-year warranty, the Pigeon Inox Pro is a neat 3-litre inner-lid option, and the Pigeon Inox stretches to 6 litres for big families. The Prestige Clip On doubles as a serving pot with its glass lid, and the Vinod Deep Pan fries like a kadai and pressure-cooks in the same vessel.

Why Stainless Steel? Steel vs Aluminium, Explained

Aluminium cookers are lighter and cheaper, and aluminium conducts heat quickly, which is why they dominated Indian kitchens for decades. The trade-offs show up over years of daily use: aluminium is a reactive metal, so long cooking of acidic foods — tomato, tamarind, lemon, vinegar-based curries — can dull the surface and affect taste; the metal also pits, stains and dents more easily, and a plain aluminium base does not work on an induction cooktop.

Stainless steel answers most of that. It is non-reactive, so acidic dishes cook and even sit in the pot without picking up a metallic taste; it does not pit or corrode under normal use, keeps its shine, and shrugs off metal spoons and rough washing. The cooking grades matter: the listings in this guide repeatedly specify 18/8 food-grade stainless steel (AISI 304) for the surface that touches food — that is the grade to look for inside the pot. Steel's one weakness is heat conduction: on its own it heats unevenly and food can catch at the base. That is why almost no good steel cooker is plain steel all the way through — the base does the clever work, as the next section explains. Steel is also heavier than aluminium, which is worth knowing if the cooker will be lifted full, every day, by someone with weak wrists.

Notable fact: induction compatibility in a steel cooker comes from a magnetic outer layer — Vinod and Hawkins both describe an SS 430 magnetic stainless steel outer layer on their tri-ply cookers, which is what lets the same pot work on gas and induction. A plain 304 steel pot would not respond to an induction hob at all.

Bases Decoded: Sandwich Bottoms and Tri-Ply

Two constructions dominate this list. A sandwich (encapsulated) bottom bonds a disc of aluminium between stainless steel sheets at the base only — the aluminium spreads heat across the floor of the pot so food does not scorch in the middle, while the body stays plain stainless steel. The Hawkins Contura SSC50 states a 6.6 mm thick sandwich bottom; the Hawkins Futura's manual describes a 7 mm base containing a 4.9 mm aluminium disc sandwiched in stainless steel; Vinod's Deep Pan simply lists a "sandwich bottom". Prestige's Alpha base on the Deluxe Alpha range is the brand's own layered base of this family — Prestige's listing for the range describes it as a triply base.

Tri-ply goes further: three layers are bonded through the whole body, base and walls alike. Vinod's Platinum listing spells the recipe out — layer 1 is AISI 304 18/8 food-grade stainless steel inside, layer 2 is encapsulated aluminium throughout for even heat distribution, and layer 3 is SS 430 magnetic stainless steel outside for induction use. Hawkins describes the same idea for its Triply range: a food-grade steel cooking surface, a heavy-gauge heat-diffusing core, and a magnetic steel outer. Tri-ply costs more, but heat climbs the walls as well as crossing the base, which helps with thicker dishes that scorch easily. Neither construction is "wrong" — a sandwich bottom is entirely adequate for dal, rice and most curries; tri-ply earns its premium in daily, heavy use.

Inner Lid vs Outer Lid

An inner-lid cooker drops the lid inside the rim of the pot, and steam pressure pushes it up against the rim to seal — the harder the pressure, the tighter the seal, which is why the style is considered inherently safe. Hawkins built its name on it. The lid needs a little room to angle in and out, so inner-lid pots suit cooking in one vessel rather than stacking multiple separators, although most families manage two separators comfortably in the larger sizes. Gaskets on inner-lid designs sit protected inside the rim; Hawkins notes for the Futura that because the lid fits from inside, the sealing ring is not rubbed sideways on every open and close and is shielded from food acids, so it lasts longer.

An outer-lid cooker clamps the lid over the top of the pot, like a cap. It is the easier style for stacking separators and for anyone who finds the inner lid's tilt-and-drop motion fiddly, and it allows designs like Prestige's Svachh deep lid, which sits deeper over the pot specifically to control frothing and spillage from foods like dal. Prestige's Clip On is a third variation: the lid clips on over the top in any direction, with no lugs to align. There is no safety gap between the styles when the cooker is genuine and ISI certified — pick the mechanism your hands prefer, because you will operate it thousands of times.

Size Guide: Which Capacity for Your Family?

Hawkins' own catalogue gives the most useful yardstick, matching its cookers to household size: a 2 litre is ideal for 2 to 3 persons, 3 litres for 3 to 4 persons, 5 litres for 5 to 7 persons and 6.5 litres for 7 to 9 persons. Treat those as cooking-for-dinner numbers, then adjust for how you actually cook. If you mostly cook rice or dal for the meal in front of you, the catalogue size is right. If you batch-cook for the week, cook for guests often, or use tall separators, go one size up — remember a pressure cooker should never be filled beyond two-thirds, and only half for foods that expand or froth, so the usable volume is always well below the headline litres. Singles and couples usually settle happily on 3 litres; a family of four to six is best served by 5 litres; joint families and heavy batch cooks should look at 6 litres and above, which in steel means the Pigeon Inox on this list.

How to Choose a Stainless Steel Pressure Cooker

  • Check for the ISI mark first. Pressure cookers sold in India should carry BIS certification — the listings here state it plainly ("ISI Certified"). It is your baseline assurance that the body, lid and safety valve have been tested as a system. Do not buy an uncertified cooker, however heavy it feels.
  • Match the base to your stove. On induction, the cooker needs a magnetic base — a tri-ply SS 430 outer layer or an induction-rated sandwich bottom, stated on the listing. On gas alone, any of these bases works. If your home might shift to induction later, buy induction-compatible now.
  • Pick the lid your hands like. Inner lid for the pressure-sealed Hawkins style, outer lid for easy separator stacking, clip-on if aligning lugs annoys you. There is no wrong answer — only the one you will use happily twice a day.
  • Read the base construction, not the adjectives. "Tri-ply" should come with the layers named (304 steel, aluminium, 430 steel). A sandwich bottom should state its thickness. If a listing cannot say what the base is made of, treat that as information.
  • Think about spares before you need them. Gaskets and vent weights are consumables. Hawkins, Prestige, Vinod, Pigeon and Butterfly all sell spares widely in India; a cooker from a brand with no local spare-parts trail becomes scrap the day the gasket perishes.
  • Weight is a feature, not a flaw — up to a point. Thick bases and steel bodies are heavy. A 5-litre steel cooker full of dal is a serious lift. If that is a concern, choose the smaller size or a sandwich-bottom model rather than tri-ply.

The 10 Best Stainless Steel Pressure Cookers at a Glance

The Best Stainless Steel Pressure Cookers in India, in Detail

1. Hawkins Triply Stainless Steel (HSST35), 3.5 Litre

Check price on Amazon

Hawkins' Triply range is the company's answer to buyers who love the classic inner-lid Hawkins but want modern, even heating. The HSST35 is the 3.5-litre size — Hawkins' catalogue logic puts that at family-of-four-to-five territory for everyday dal, rice and sabzi — in a wide body with the familiar loop-lock inner lid and a pressure-locked safety design. The Amazon.in listing confirms the essentials: stainless steel construction, an induction compatible base, a locking lid, and compatibility with gas, electric and induction stovetops.

The tri-ply construction is the point of the model. As Hawkins describes its Triply cookers, the cooking surface is 18/8 superior food-grade stainless steel, a heavy-gauge heat-diffusing metal core spreads heat evenly through the base and up the sides, and the outer layer is AISI 430 magnetic stainless steel, which is what makes the pot induction-friendly. In practice that means fewer scorched patches at the bottom of a thick dal and no need for a separate induction plate. At 2.2 kg it is a solid, confidence-inspiring thing rather than a lightweight — allow for that if it will be lifted by elderly hands.

Notable fact: retail listings for the HSST35 carry Hawkins' 5-year guarantee on the steel cooker, and the safety design pairs the inner-fitting, pressure-locked lid with a locking loop — the lid physically cannot be lifted while pressure holds it sealed from inside.

Key Details

  • Capacity: 3.5 litres
  • Lid Type: Inner lid, locking loop
  • Construction: Tri-ply — 18/8 food-grade stainless steel inner, heat-diffusing core, AISI 430 magnetic stainless steel outer
  • Stove Compatibility: Gas, induction and electric (per Amazon.in listing)
  • Item Weight: 2.2 kg (per Amazon.in listing)
  • Warranty: 5 years (per retail listing)

2. Hawkins Contura Stainless Steel (SSC50), 5 Litre

Check price on Amazon

If one cooker on this list deserves the word "default", it is the Contura SSC50. The curved Contura body — wider at the belly, easy to stir and scrape — is executed here in stainless steel with Hawkins' inner lid, at the 5-litre size the listing recommends for 5 to 7 persons. Safety and Care: Getting Decades Out of a Steel Cooker

Start with certification and fill levels, because they prevent nearly every cooker accident. Buy only ISI-certified cookers — every model in this guide states the mark — and respect the fill lines: Hawkins' manuals put it plainly, never fill the cooker more than two-thirds full, no more than half for foods that expand during cooking such as rice and dried vegetables, and no more than one-third for dals and pulses that sprout and froth. Several litres of "spare" capacity is not wasted space; it is the safety margin that keeps the vent clear.

Maintenance is mostly gasket and vent discipline. Wash the gasket after use and replace it when it hardens, cracks or starts leaking steam at the rim — a leaking gasket is a worn gasket, not a faulty cooker. Keep the whistle and vent pipe clear: after cooking frothy dals, check the vent is not clogged before the next use, because a blocked vent is how pressure misbehaves. If a fusible safety valve ever operates, it has done its one job — replace it with a genuine spare before cooking again, and, as Hawkins' manual insists, always use genuine spare parts for your model. Never force a lid open while pressure remains; let the cooker cool or release pressure as the design intends. The steel body itself asks for almost nothing: wash it like any steel vessel, dry it to avoid water marks, and a paste of baking soda lifts the occasional scorched patch without scratching.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a stainless steel pressure cooker better than an aluminium one?

For most homes, yes — with a small trade-off. Steel is non-reactive with acidic foods, does not pit or stain, has no coating to wear, and (with a magnetic base) works on induction. Aluminium is lighter and cheaper and heats a little faster, but it can react with acidic dishes over long cooking and dents more easily. Steel costs more upfront and lasts considerably longer.

What does tri-ply actually mean?

Three layers bonded together through the whole body of the cooker: food-grade stainless steel (usually 18/8, AISI 304) on the inside, aluminium in the middle to spread heat evenly, and magnetic stainless steel (SS 430) outside so the pot works on induction. A sandwich-bottom cooker puts the same idea only in the base, which is enough for most cooking and costs less.

Will every stainless steel cooker work on an induction stove?

No. Induction needs a magnetic base. Cookers built with an SS 430 outer layer or an induction-rated sandwich bottom work; a plain stainless pot may not be detected by the hob at all. Check that the listing states induction compatibility — every model in this guide was chosen with its stove compatibility verified, and the table notes it where the listing states it.

Which size should a family of four buy?

Five litres is the safe family size — Hawkins' catalogue rates 5 litres for 5 to 7 persons, and a family of four that cooks rice and dal together, or likes leftovers, will use the room. If you mostly cook one dish at a time for immediate eating, 3.5 litres serves four comfortably and takes less cupboard space.

Inner lid or outer lid — which is safer?

Both are safe in a genuine, ISI-certified cooker; they seal differently. An inner lid is pushed tighter by the pressure itself and protects its gasket inside the rim. An outer lid clamps over the top and is easier for stacking separators. Choose by handling preference — and never buy an uncertified cooker of either type.
